• Follows a diurnal rhythm peaking in the early morning

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient presents with hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and hyponatremia. Laboratory tests confirm adrenal cortex dysfunction with failure to respond to ACTH. Identify the diagnosis.
back:
• Addison Disease (Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency)
• Requires replacement of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids
• Hydrocortisone is the standard treatment

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain how the dexamethasone suppression test distinguishes normal individuals from those with Cushing syndrome.
back:
• Normal: Dexamethasone provides negative feedback to suppress pituitary ACTH and cortisol.
• Cushing Syndrome: The feedback loop is disrupted; cortisol remains high despite dexamethasone administration.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency with Secondary/Tertiary Insufficiency regarding mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) levels.
back:
• Primary: Adrenal cortex is destroyed; both cortisol and aldosterone are deficient.
• Secondary/Tertiary: Pituitary/Hypothalamic defect; aldosterone is mostly preserved as it is regulated by Renin-Angiotensin.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Detail the pharmacological step and clinical goal for administering betamethasone intramuscularly to a mother in preterm labor at 32 weeks' gestation.
back:
• Goal: Accelerate fetal lung maturation
• Mechanism: Stimulates production of pulmonary surfactant
• Reduces risk of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: The most common serious adverse effect of chronic glucocorticoid therapy, requiring prophylactic calcium and vitamin D supplementation, is [___].
back:
• Osteoporosis
• Caused by inhibited intestinal calcium absorption and suppressed bone formation
• Bisphosphonates may be used for treatment

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: An expectant mother requires steroid therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. Why is Prednisone specifically preferred over Prednisolone in this scenario?
back:
• Prednisone is a prodrug
• Placental enzymes convert active prednisolone back to inactive prednisone
• Protects the fetus from systemic steroid effects

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient with hyperaldosteronism develops gynecomastia after starting Spironolactone. Explain why switching to Eplerenone is the appropriate management.
back:
• Spironolactone: Non-selective; antagonizes aldosterone and androgen receptors (causing gynecomastia).
• Eplerenone: Highly selective for mineralocorticoid receptors; lacks anti-androgen side effects.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast the standard replacement dosing schedule of hydrocortisone to mimic the physiological diurnal metabolic loop.
back:
• Total dose is divided into two parts
• 2/3 dose given in the early morning (peak)
• 1/3 dose given in the late afternoon (secondary peak)

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Identify the specific adrenal zone responsible for aldosterone production and its primary physiological trigger.
back:
• Zona Glomerulosa (outer zone)
• Triggered by the Renin-Angiotensin System
• Regulates salt and water metabolism

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Corticosteroids exert their metabolic and anti-inflammatory effects by binding to specific [___] receptors, which then translocate to the nucleus to act as transcription factors.
back:
Intracellular cytoplasmic
* Receptors dimerize after ligand binding.
* They interact with glucocorticoid response elements (GRE) to regulate gene expression.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient with Addison disease remains hypotensive and hyponatremic despite hydrocortisone therapy. Identify the specific synthetic mineralocorticoid that should be added to manage this electrolyte imbalance.
back:
Fludrocortisone
* Provides potent salt-retaining activity.
* Used to supplement mineralocorticoid deficiency when hydrocortisone alone is insufficient.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain the biochemical rationale for administering Leucovorin (folinic acid) in combination with 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) during cancer chemotherapy.
back:
Potentiates 5-FU activity
* Provides the reduced folate coenzyme (5,10-methylene-THF) needed.
* Stabilizes the ternary complex between thymidylate synthase and FdUMP, enhancing enzyme inhibition.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Distinguish between the receptor-binding profiles of Spironolactone and Eplerenone regarding their propensity to cause gynecomastia in male patients.
back:
Spironolactone: Non-selective; antagonizes both mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors (causes gynecomastia).
* Eplerenone: Selective for mineralocorticoid receptors; lacks anti-androgenic effects.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Specify the most characteristic dose-limiting toxicity associated with Vincristine that distinguishes it from its structural analog, Vinblastine.
back:
Peripheral Neuropathy
* Manifests as paresthesias, loss of reflexes, and foot drop.
* Vincristine is notably less myelosuppressive than Vinblastine.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: In the management of premature labor, [___] is administered intramuscularly to the mother to accelerate fetal lung maturation and reduce the risk of respiratory distress syndrome.
back:
Betamethasone or Dexamethasone
* Both agents cross the placenta efficiently.
* They stimulate the production of surfactant in the fetal lungs.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A 55-year-old male receiving high-dose Ifosfamide therapy develops gross hematuria. Name the cytoprotective agent that must be administered to neutralize the metabolite responsible for this condition.
back:
Mesna (Sodium 2-mercaptoethane sulfonate)
* Binds and neutralizes acrolein in the bladder.
* Aggressive hydration is also required to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain why Tamoxifen is classified as a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM) rather than a pure estrogen antagonist.
back:
Tissue-specific activity
* Antagonist in breast tissue (inhibits tumor growth).
* Partial agonist in bone (prevents resorption) and endometrium (increases risk of hyperplasia).

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast the primary dose-limiting toxicities of the platinum coordination complexes Cisplatin and Carboplatin.
back:
Cisplatin: Nephrotoxicity and severe nausea/vomiting.
* Carboplatin: Myelosuppression (primarily thrombocytopenia).
* Cisplatin requires vigorous pre-hydration; Carboplatin does not.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
coreConcept: Ketoconazole as a Steroid Synthesis Inhibitor
front: Identify the antifungal agent utilized in high doses to treat Cushing syndrome due to its ability to nonselectively inhibit adrenal steroidogenesis.
back:
Ketoconazole
* Inhibits P450 enzymes (e.g., 11β-hydroxylase and 17α-hydroxylase).
* Effectively blocks the synthesis of all adrenal and gonadal steroids.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The nucleoside analog [___] is clinically recognized as a potent radiosensitizer, often used in pancreatic cancer to enhance the lethal effects of ionizing radiation.
back:
Gemcitabine.
- Inhibits DNA synthesis and repair.
- Enhances radiation-induced cell death.
- Commonly used in pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancer protocols.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A 55-year-old male undergoing radiotherapy for a glioblastoma develops signs of increased intracranial pressure. The glucocorticoid of choice to manage this peritumoral edema is [___].
back:
Dexamethasone.
- High glucocorticoid potency with minimal mineralocorticoid activity.
- Reduces capillary permeability in the blood-brain barrier.
- Standard treatment for CNS radiation-induced edema.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the pharmacological rationale for combining Mitomycin C with radiotherapy in the treatment of solid tumors like squamous cell carcinoma.
back:
- Targets hypoxic tumor cells.
- Undergoes reductive activation to form a DNA-crosslinking alkylating agent.
- Complements radiation, which primarily kills well-oxygenated cells via free radicals.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the utility of Cetuximab versus traditional cytotoxic agents when used concurrently with radiation in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
back:
Cetuximab:
- Targeted IgG1 monoclonal antibody against EGFR.
- Enhances radiation response without typical myelosuppression.
Cytotoxics:
- Broad DNA damage.
- Higher risk of systemic hematopoietic toxicity.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Certain antitumor antibiotics like Doxorubicin are known to cause 'Radiation Recall.' Describe the clinical presentation of this phenomenon.
back:
- Inflammatory skin reaction at a previously irradiated site.
- Triggered by subsequent administration of chemotherapy.
- Manifests as erythema, blistering, or desquamation of the skin.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: In the neoadjuvant treatment of locally advanced rectal cancer, the fluoropyrimidine [___] is the standard drug used concurrently with radiation to achieve tumor downstaging.
back:
5-Fluorouracil (or oral Capecitabine).
- Acts as a radiosensitizer.
- Depletes thymidine pools needed for DNA repair.
- Increases the likelihood of complete surgical resection.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with anal cancer receives 5-Fluorouracil and Mitomycin during their radiation course. Identify the specific cellular environment where Mitomycin is most active compared to radiation.
back:
Hypoxic environments.
- Radiation requires oxygen to form DNA-damaging free radicals.
- Mitomycin is preferentially activated in low-oxygen (reductive) tumor cores.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Describe the molecular mechanism by which 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) enhances the efficacy of ionizing radiation during concurrent therapy.
back:
- Inhibits Thymidylate Synthase (TS).
- Depletes deoxythymidine triphosphate (dTTP).
- Hinders the repair of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Distinguish between the primary goals of Radiosensitizers and Radioprotectors in clinical oncology.
back:
Radiosensitizers (e.g., Gemcitabine):
- Increase the sensitivity of tumor cells to radiation damage.
Radioprotectors:
- Protect normal non-neoplastic tissues from radiation-induced injury.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the specific enzyme whose genetic deficiency leads to life-threatening toxicity when a patient receives 5-Fluorouracil as a radiosensitizer.
back:
Dihydropyrimidine Dehydrogenase (DPD).
- Responsible for >80% of 5-FU catabolism.
- Deficiency leads to severe myelosuppression, neurotoxicity, and enteritis.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: In the treatment of pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancer, the pyrimidine analog [___] is utilized as a potent radiosensitizer to enhance the efficacy of ionizing radiation.
back: * Gemcitabine. • Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. • Competes with dCTP for DNA polymerase. • Promotes radiation-induced DNA strand breakage.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with squamous cell anal cancer is prescribed a drug specifically designed to target the hypoxic tumor stem cells that are typically resistant to radiation. Name this agent.
back: * Mitomycin (Mitomycin C). • Undergoes metabolic activation in reductive/hypoxic environments. • Cross-links DNA to trigger cell death. • Used concurrently with radiation therapy.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the mechanism by which Dexamethasone is used to manage side effects during the radiation phase for intracranial malignancies.
back: * Reduces peritumoral edema. • Stabilizes the blood-brain barrier. • Decreases capillary permeability. • Lacks mineralocorticoid activity, minimizing fluid/electrolyte complications.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Dexamethasone and Hydrocortisone in the context of radiation-induced cerebral edema.
back: * Dexamethasone: Long-acting, potent anti-inflammatory, minimal salt retention; preferred for edema. • Hydrocortisone: Short-acting, high salt-retaining activity; used for replacement, not edema.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Which specific monoclonal antibody is indicated for concurrent administration with radiotherapy in patients presenting with locally advanced head and neck cancer?
back: * Cetuximab. • Targets the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). • Enhances cellular response to radiation. • Interferes with growth and repair pathways.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The platinum coordination complex [___] is often preferred in radiotherapy combinations because it provides synergistic cytotoxicity by inhibiting DNA repair and polymerases.
back: * Cisplatin. • Forms intrastrand DNA cross-links. • Acts as a chemical radiosensitizer. • Requires aggressive hydration to prevent nephrotoxicity.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient previously treated with Doxorubicin presents with severe erythema limited to a new radiation field. Name this drug-radiation interaction.
back: * Radiation Recall Reaction. • Latent tissue injury triggered by Anthracyclines. • Manifests as inflammatory desquamation. • Occurs strictly at prior radiation sites.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Describe the molecular risk associated with the concurrent administration of Bleomycin and thoracic radiation therapy.
back: * Synergistic pulmonary toxicity. • Both agents induce oxidative DNA damage and free radicals. • Leads to irreversible pulmonary fibrosis (‘Bleomycin lung’).

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Distinguish between Neoadjuvant and Adjuvant drug administration phases when used in combination with radiotherapy.
back: * Neoadjuvant: Given before radiation/surgery to debulk primary tumors. • Adjuvant: Given after local treatment to target occult micrometastases.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: State the primary pharmacologic purpose of a 'radiosensitizer' during the management of large solid tumor masses.
back: * Increases tumor cell killing per radiation dose. • Promotes cells into the sensitive G2/M phase. • Overcomes resistance in poorly vascularized regions.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The antimetabolite commonly used in pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancer as a potent radiosensitizer is [___].
back:
### **Gemcitabine**
*  Acts as a potent radiosensitizer.
*  Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and DNA repair mechanisms.
*  Used concurrently with radiotherapy to enhance tumor kill.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with anal squamous cell carcinoma is prescribed an agent to specifically target radioresistant hypoxic tumor stem cells. Identify the drug.
back:
### **Mitomycin**
*  Activated by enzyme-mediated reduction in hypoxic environments.
*  Functions as a bifunctional alkylating agent.
*  Targets hypoxic cells that are typically resistant to radiation.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the synergistic mechanism between Cisplatin and ionizing radiation during cancer treatment.
back:
### **Cisplatin Synergism**
*  Inhibits the repair of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks.
*  Forms platinum-DNA adducts that sensitize cells to lethal damage.
*  Synchronizes the cell cycle to more radiosensitive phases.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the therapeutic objectives of Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy versus Adjuvant Chemotherapy in patients receiving radiotherapy.
back:
### **Neoadjuvant vs. Adjuvant**
*  **Neoadjuvant:** Administered *before* radiotherapy/surgery to debulk the primary tumor.
*  **Adjuvant:** Administered *after* local treatment to eradicate systemic micrometastases.
*  Both aim to improve long-term disease-free survival.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the specific glucocorticoid used to manage cerebral edema caused by brain tumors or radiotherapy.
back:
### **Dexamethasone**
*  Potent anti-inflammatory with minimal mineralocorticoid activity.
*  Reduces intracranial pressure and radiation-induced neurotoxicity.
*  Stabilizes the blood-brain barrier to minimize fluid leakage.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: EGFR Inhibition in Combined Modality Therapy
front: During radiation for head and neck cancers, the monoclonal antibody that enhances therapeutic efficacy by targeting EGFR is [___].
back:
### **Cetuximab**
*  Targets the extracellular domain of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor.
*  Blocks downstream signaling involved in cell growth and survival.
*  Synergizes with radiation to improve local control rates.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with rectal cancer receives a 12-week course of 5-Fluorouracil concurrently with pelvic radiation. Describe the pharmacological role of 5-FU in this scenario.
back:
### **Concurrent Radiopotentiation**
*  Inhibits thymidylate synthase to deplete thymidine pools.
*  Interferes with the repair of radiation-induced sublethal DNA damage.
*  Increases the therapeutic efficacy of the local radiation dose.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Detail the mechanism by which hypoxic environments facilitate the activation of Mitomycin in combined modality therapy.
back:
### **Hypoxic Reductive Activation**
*  Undergoes bioreductive activation in low-oxygen tumor cores.
*  Creates reactive species that cross-link DNA strands.
*  Selectively kills cells that are protected from oxygen-dependent radiation damage.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Distinguish between a Radiosensitizer and a Radioprotector in terms of the therapeutic index.
back:
### **Therapeutic Index Modulation**
*  **Radiosensitizer:** Enhances tumor cell kill, shifting the tumor-response curve to the left.
*  **Radioprotector:** Protects normal tissue from damage, shifting the toxicity curve to the right.
*  Both aim to widen the therapeutic window.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: List two pharmacological factors that determine the selection of drugs for combined modality (Chemo-Radiation) protocols.
back:
### **Protocol Selection Factors**
*  **Non-overlapping Toxicity:** Drugs should not worsen radiation-induced organ damage.
*  **Intrinsic Radiosensitivity:** Agents must independently possess activity against the specific tumor type.
*  **Optimal Scheduling:** Must align drug peaks with radiation fractions.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The chemotherapeutic agent [___] is uniquely effective against hypoxic tumor stem cells and is frequently used as a radiosensitizer in squamous cell anal cancer.
back: Mitomycin C. • Acts as an alkylating agent forming DNA cross-links. • Targets relatively anaerobic tumor centers. • Synergizes with radiation to kill oxygen-deprived cells.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient undergoing chemotherapy for breast cancer develops severe erythema and desquamation at a skin site previously treated with radiotherapy months ago. Identify this clinical phenomenon.
back: Radiation Recall Reaction. • Often triggered by Doxorubicin (Anthracyclines). • Inflammatory skin response at prior radiation fields. • Occurs weeks to months after radiotherapy completion.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the role of Cisplatin in enhancing the biological efficacy of concurrent ionizing radiation during the treatment of head and neck cancers.
back: • Forms DNA cross-links that inhibit cellular repair mechanisms. • Synchronizes tumor cells into the G1/S phases of the cell cycle. • Increases the lethal effect of radiation-induced DNA strand breaks.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the primary therapeutic goals of 'Neoadjuvant' chemotherapy versus 'Adjuvant' chemotherapy when utilized in a combined modality plan with radiotherapy.
back: • Neoadjuvant: Given BEFORE radiation to shrink the primary tumor mass. • Adjuvant: Given AFTER radiation to eradicate occult micrometastases and prevent systemic recurrence.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the nucleoside analog that acts as a potent radiosensitizer in pancreatic cancer treatment, despite increasing the risk of local tissue toxicity.
back: Gemcitabine. • Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. • Competes with deoxycytidine for DNA incorporation. • Halts DNA repair after radiation-induced damage.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: During cranial radiotherapy for high-grade gliomas, the corticosteroid [___] is administered as a standard adjunct to manage peritumoral edema.
back: Dexamethasone. • Potent glucocorticoid with minimal salt-retaining activity. • Stabilizes the blood-brain barrier. • Reduces capillary permeability and intracranial pressure.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A 24-year-old male with testicular cancer is treated with Bleomycin. Describe why a history of prior thoracic irradiation significantly increases his risk for fatal pulmonary complications.
back: Potentiation of Pulmonary Fibrosis. • Bleomycin induces oxygen free radicals. • Prior radiation damages lung parenchyma and reduces repair capacity. • Synergism leads to progressive pneumonitis and fibrosis.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain how Cetuximab acts as a targeted adjunct to radiotherapy in the management of locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma.
back: • Binds to the Extracellular Domain of EGFR. • Inhibits downstream pro-survival signaling. • Prevents radiation-induced activation of growth factors that contribute to radioresistance.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Distinguish between the protective roles of Mesna and Dexrazoxane when used alongside high-dose cytotoxic therapy.
back: • Mesna: Neutralizes acrolein to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis from Cyclophosphamide. • Dexrazoxane: Chelates iron to prevent Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: State the primary implication of the 'Log-Kill Hypothesis' for a patient with a large, clinically detectable tumor mass receiving chemotherapy.
back: • Drugs kill a constant fraction (percentage) of cells, not a fixed number. • Higher tumor burdens require more cycles of therapy. • Cure is more likely when tumor burden is low.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: The principal endogenous human glucocorticoid synthesized in the zona fasciculata that promotes gluconeogenesis and increases resistance to stress is [___].
back: • Cortisol (Hydrocortisone) • Secreted in a diurnal rhythm peaking early in the morning • Functions as the primary feedback inhibitor of ACTH and CRH secretion

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A 45-year-old female in physical rehabilitation for rheumatoid arthritis has been on high-dose Prednisone for six months. She presents with proximal muscle weakness, purple striae, and moon face. Identify the most likely metabolic bone complication.
back: • Glucocorticoid-induced Osteoporosis • Caused by inhibited intestinal calcium absorption and suppressed bone formation • Patients often require Calcium, Vitamin D, or Bisphosphonates

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which glucocorticoids inhibit the production of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
back: • Induction of lipocortins (annexins) • Direct inhibition of Phospholipase A2 • Prevents the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast the salt-retaining activity and duration of action of Hydrocortisone with Dexamethasone in the context of inflammatory disease management.
back: • Hydrocortisone: Short-acting (8-12 hours) with significant salt-retaining (mineralocorticoid) activity • Dexamethasone: Long-acting (36-55 hours) with zero salt-retaining activity • Dexamethasone has 25-30 times higher anti-inflammatory potency

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Detail the pharmacological rationale for preferring Prednisone over other glucocorticoids during pregnancy.
back: • Prednisone is a prodrug not activated by the fetal liver • Placental enzymes convert active Prednisolone back into inactive Prednisone • This mechanism protects the fetus from systemic steroid effects

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Regarding rehabilitative safety in pregnancy, the corticosteroid [___] is preferred because it is a prodrug that cannot be converted to its active form in the fetal liver.
back:
Prednisone. 
- Minimized fetal effects. 
- Converted to active Prednisolone by maternal liver. 
- Placental enzymes inactivate active forms back to Prednisone.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A woman in preterm labor at 30 weeks gestation is given a corticosteroid injection to prevent fetal respiratory distress syndrome. Name the drug and its rehabilitative goal.
back:
Betamethasone (or Dexamethasone). 
- Accelerates fetal lung maturation. 
- Stimulates surfactant production. 
- Administered intramuscularly to the mother.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Describe the multi-step enzymatic inhibition performed by Ketoconazole when used as an anti-adrenal agent in Cushing syndrome.
back:
Non-selective steroid synthesis inhibition. 
- Inhibits cholesterol side-chain cleavage. 
- Blocks P450c11 and 3̧-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase. 
- Reduces both gonadal and adrenal hormone production.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast the replacement requirements for primary adrenocortical insufficiency (Addison's) versus secondary insufficiency regarding mineralocorticoid therapy.
back:
Primary: Requires both Hydrocortisone and Fludrocortisone. 
- Secondary: Requires only Hydrocortisone. 
- In secondary, the renin-angiotensin system maintains adequate aldosterone levels despite pituitary failure.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Identify the clinical classification for chemotherapy administered after a rehabilitative surgical resection to eradicate occult micrometastases.
back:
Adjuvant chemotherapy. 
- Goal is to prevent recurrence. 
- Reduces systemic relapse risk. 
- Administered after local control (surgery/radiation).

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: To prevent the rehabilitative complication of hemorrhagic cystitis during Ifosfamide or high-dose Cyclophosphamide therapy, the sulfhydryl compound [___] is administered.
back:
Mesna. 
- Neutralizes acrolein in the bladder. 
- Requires adequate patient hydration. 
- Prevents bladder fibrosis.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma receives a chimeric monoclonal antibody that recruits immune effector functions against B lymphocytes. Identify the target of this drug.
back:
CD20 antigen. 
- Drug: Rituximab. 
- Causes complement-mediated cytotoxicity. 
- Targets both normal and malignant B cells.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain the anti-angiogenesis mechanism of Bevacizumab regarding its interaction with the Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF).
back:
VEGF-A ligand sequestration. 
- Prevents binding to VEGFR receptors. 
- Inhibits new blood vessel formation. 
- Starves tumors of nutrients and oxygen.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Distinguish between the mechanisms of Tamoxifen and Letrozole in the treatment of postmenopausal hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer.
back:
Tamoxifen: Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM). 
- Letrozole: Aromatase Inhibitor (blocks synthesis). 
- Letrozole is preferred in postmenopausal women. 
- Tamoxifen carries risk of endometrial cancer.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: In the management of Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia (CML), identify the specific molecular 'pocket' occupied by Imatinib to prevent signal transduction.
back:
Kinase pocket (ATP-binding site). 
- Target: Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase. 
- Prevents substrate phosphorylation. 
- Inhibits leukemic cell proliferation.

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: The synthetic mineralocorticoid [___] is primarily utilized in replacement therapy to supplement salt-retaining activity in patients with Addison's disease.
back:
* Fludrocortisone
* High mineralocorticoid-to-glucocorticoid potency ratio
* Essential for regulating salt and water metabolism
* Prevents hyponatremia and hyperkalemia

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient with fatigue and hyperpigmentation presents with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. After an ACTH stimulation test shows no cortisol response, identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
* Primary Adrenocortical Insufficiency (Addison's Disease)
* Caused by adrenal cortex dysfunction
* Requires glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement
* Failure to treat is potentially fatal

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Explain how glucocorticoids inhibit the production of prostaglandins and leukotrienes at the enzymatic level to reduce inflammation during rehabilitation.
back:
* Inhibition of Phospholipase A2
* Prevents release of arachidonic acid from membranes
* Arachidonic acid is the essential precursor for inflammatory mediators
* Leads to decreased prostaglandin/leukotriene synthesis

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A clinician must choose between Betamethasone and Hydrocortisone for an inflammatory flare in a patient with comorbid congestive heart failure. Contrast these agents regarding their salt-retaining properties.
back:
* Betamethasone: Long-acting (36-54h); Zero mineralocorticoid (salt-retaining) activity
* Hydrocortisone: Short-acting (1-12h); Significant mineralocorticoid activity (ratio 1:1)
* Betamethasone is safer for patients requiring strict fluid/electrolyte control

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Identify the pharmacological rationale for preferring Prednisone over Prednisolone when treating a pregnant patient to minimize corticosteroid exposure to the fetus.
back:
* Prednisone is an inactive pro-drug
* Maternal liver activates it to prednisolone
* Placental enzymes biotransform prednisolone back to inactive prednisone
* Fetal liver cannot re-activate prednisone

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: To diagnose Cushing's syndrome, the synthetic glucocorticoid [___] is administered because it typically suppresses cortisol release in healthy individuals but fails to do so in hypercortisolism cases.
back:
* Dexamethasone
* Utilized in the Dexamethasone Suppression Test
* Potent long-acting glucocorticoid
* Zero mineralocorticoid activity

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: A patient undergoing long-term steroid therapy for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops centripetal fat distribution, a 'buffalo hump,' and thinning skin. Identify the underlying pathophysiology.
back:
* Iatrogenic Cushing's Syndrome
* Result of chronic excess exogenous glucocorticoids
* Causes protein catabolism and redistribution of body fat
* Associated with moon facies and purple striae

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Describe the molecular role of the hGR-beta isoform in patients exhibiting partial glucocorticoid resistance compared to the classic hGR-alpha receptor.
back:
* hGR-beta is a transcriptionally inactive isoform
* Acts as an endogenous inhibitor of hGR-alpha
* Does not bind glucocorticoids directly
* High levels result in reduced tissue sensitivity to steroids

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Contrast the metabolic effects of glucocorticoids on protein in the liver versus protein in lymphoid and connective tissues.
back:
* Liver: Stimulates RNA and protein synthesis
* Peripheral Tissues: Catabolic/Antianabolic effects (protein breakdown)
* Results in muscle wasting and skin thinning
* Increases available amino acids for gluconeogenesis

category: Discuss the drugs related to rehabilitation
front: Specify the exact histological zone of the adrenal cortex responsible for the synthesis of cortisol and other glucocorticoids.
back:
* Zona Fasciculata
* The middle layer of the adrenal cortex
* Regulated primarily by pituitary ACTH
* Synthesizes steroids from cholesterol

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: In the treatment of various solid tumors, the antimetabolite [___] is frequently utilized as a potent radiosensitizer to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of ionizing radiation.
back: * Gemcitabine. * Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase. * Depletes deoxyribonucleotide pools. * Facilitates radiation-induced DNA strand breakage.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with locally advanced head and neck cancer is scheduled for concurrent chemotherapy and radiation. Explain the pathophysiological advantage of adding Cisplatin to this regimen.
back: * Synergistic cytotoxicity. * Inhibits repair of radiation-induced DNA damage. * Creates platinum-DNA adducts. * Enhances tumor cell kill in the primary site.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: Mitomycin C and Hypoxic Cell Targeting
front: Describe the specific pharmacological advantage of using Mitomycin C in combination with radiotherapy for the treatment of large, solid tumor masses.
back: * Targets hypoxic tumor cells. * Acts as a bioreductive alkylating agent. * Activated in low-oxygen environments. * Complements radiation, which primarily kills oxygenated cells.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the radiosensitizing mechanisms of Gemcitabine and 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) when employed in combined modality oncology protocols.
back: * Gemcitabine: Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and reduces dNTP pools. * 5-FU: Inhibits thymidylate synthase and incorporates into RNA. * Both maximize DNA damage when cells are irradiated.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: State the clinical purpose of administering high-dose corticosteroids, such as Dexamethasone, during the management of brain tumors undergoing radiation therapy.
back: * Reduces peritumoral edema. * Mitigates increased intracranial pressure. * Decreases inflammatory responses to irradiation. * Stabilizes the blood-brain barrier.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: In the management of locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck, the monoclonal antibody [___] is combined with radiotherapy to target growth signaling.
back: * Cetuximab. * Targets Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR). * Inhibits downstream proliferation signals. * Sensitizes tumor cells to radiation-induced apoptosis.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A 50-year-old patient receives a cytoprotectant agent before beginning a course of pelvic radiation. What is the intended biological effect of this pharmacological intervention?
back: * Selective protection of healthy tissue. * Reduces radiation-induced side effects like proctitis. * Scavenges free radicals in non-malignant cells. * Does not compromise the tumor's response.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain how topoisomerase I inhibitors, such as Topotecan or Irinotecan, interact with ionizing radiation to cause lethality in cancer cells.
back: * Stabilizes the cleavable DNA-enzyme complex. * Prevents re-ligation of single-strand breaks. * Radiation induces further DNA fragmentation. * Leads to lethal, irreversible double-strand breaks during replication.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: Temporal Phases of Combined Modality Therapy
front: Distinguish between the neoadjuvant and adjuvant phases of pharmacological therapy in a patient undergoing a combined-modality plan including radiation and surgery.
back: * Neoadjuvant: Drugs given before surgery/radiation to debulk tumors. * Adjuvant: Drugs given after local therapy to target micrometastases. * Neoadjuvant often improves surgical resectability.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the primary high-yield reason for incorporating 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) into the treatment of locally advanced rectal cancer during the radiotherapy phase.
back: * Functions as a radiosensitizer. * Improves local control rates. * Facilitates organ-sparing or sphincter-preserving surgery. * Enhances DNA damage induced by pelvic irradiation.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The antimetabolite [___] is recognized as a potent radiosensitizer, frequently used in combined modality therapy for pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancers to enhance radiation-induced DNA damage.
back:
• Gemcitabine
• Fluorine-substituted deoxycytidine analog
• Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, depleting dNTP pools
• Blocks DNA repair and induces S-phase arrest

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with glioblastoma multiforme undergoing radiotherapy develops signs of increased intracranial pressure. The primary steroid administered to manage this radiation-induced peritumoral edema is [___].
back:
• Dexamethasone
• High glucocorticoid potency with minimal mineralocorticoid activity
• Reduces blood-brain barrier permeability and cerebral edema
• Minimizes systemic fluid retention compared to hydrocortisone

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the biological rationale for utilizing Mitomycin in conjunction with radiotherapy for the management of squamous cell carcinomas (e.g., anal or head and neck cancers).
back:
• Targets hypoxic tumor stem cells
• Requires reductive activation (favored in oxygen-poor environments)
• Functions as an alkylating agent to cross-link DNA
• Eradicates radiation-resistant cells in poorly vascularized tumor regions

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of 'Radiation Recall' induced by Anthracyclines (e.g., Doxorubicin) with standard acute radiation dermatitis.
back:
• Recall: Inflammatory reaction at a previously irradiated site triggered by subsequent chemotherapy
• Standard: Acute skin toxicity occurring during or immediately after radiation exposure
• Associated Drugs: Doxorubicin and Bleomycin
• Mechanism: Delayed hypersensitivity or localized tissue sensitivity

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Detail the clinical benefit of the synergistic interaction between Cisplatin and ionizing radiation in the treatment of locally advanced solid tumors.
back:
• Acts as a chemical radiosensitizer
• Inhibits cellular DNA repair mechanisms following radiation-induced breaks
• Forms platinum-DNA adducts (Guanine N7)
• Improves local tumor control and curative potential in cervical/head and neck cancers

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The antimetabolite [___] is commonly utilized as a potent radiosensitizer in the combined modality treatment of pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancer.
back:
Gemcitabine
* Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase, depleting dNTP pools.
* Blocks DNA synthesis and repair polymerases.
* Potentiates radiation-induced programmed cell death in solid tumors.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the anus receives an antibiotic agent during radiotherapy that specifically targets hypoxic tumor stem cells. Name the agent and its primary mechanism.
back:
Mitomycin (C)
* Acts as a bifunctional alkylating agent.
* Forms DNA cross-links following reductive activation.
* Highly effective against hypoxic cells in poorly vascularized tumor regions.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the role of Dexamethasone in the management of patients undergoing radiotherapy for primary or metastatic brain tumors.
back:
Cerebral Edema Management
* Reduces intracranial pressure and peri-tumoral edema.
* Decreases capillary permeability in the brain.
* Provides immediate symptomatic relief during acute radiation phases.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: Platinum Analog Selection in Renal Dysfunction
front: A 60-year-old patient with bladder cancer requires radiosensitizing chemotherapy but has a baseline creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min. Contrast the choice between Cisplatin and Carboplatin in this scenario.
back:
Carboplatin vs. Cisplatin
* Cisplatin: Highly nephrotoxic; contraindicated in significant renal impairment.
* Carboplatin: Better tolerated renally; dose-limiting toxicity is myelosuppression.
* Both create DNA cross-links to enhance radiation efficacy.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Why is Leucovorin (folinic acid) specifically combined with 5-Fluorouracil during the chemoradiotherapy phase of colorectal cancer treatment?
back:
Potentiation of Thymidylate Synthase Inhibition
* Provides the essential reduced folate coenzyme.
* Stabilizes the ternary complex with thymidylate synthase.
* Enhances DNA synthesis blockade and radiation sensitivity.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A rare but serious complication of Mitomycin therapy, occasionally seen during combined modality regimens and characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, is [___].
back:
Hemolytic-Uremic Syndrome (HUS)
* Presents with thrombocytopenia and progressive renal failure.
* Results from microvascular damage.
* Requires immediate cessation of the offending agent.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient undergoing pelvic radiotherapy receives Prednisone to manage inflammatory symptoms. Describe the risk of abrupt discontinuation of this drug after three weeks of therapy.
back:
Acute Adrenal Insufficiency
* Caused by HPA axis suppression.
* Abrupt withdrawal prevents adrenal recovery.
* Symptoms include hypotension, nausea, and potential circulatory shock.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Describe the molecular interaction between platinum coordination complexes and DNA that leads to increased tumor cell lethality when combined with ionizing radiation.
back:
DNA Cross-linking
* Binds covalently to N7 position of guanine.
* Forms interstrand and intrastrand cross-links.
* Inhibits DNA polymerases, preventing repair of radiation-induced strand breaks.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the clinical goals of neoadjuvant versus adjuvant chemotherapy phases in a patient with locally advanced rectal cancer undergoing radiotherapy.
back:
Neoadjuvant vs. Adjuvant
* Neoadjuvant: Shrinks primary tumor before surgery/radiation to improve resectability.
* Adjuvant: Eradicates occult micrometastases after local treatment.
* Both aim to improve disease-free survival.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the genetic condition that puts a patient at risk for life-threatening toxicity when receiving 5-Fluorouracil-based chemoradiotherapy.
back:
Dihydropyrimidine Dehydrogenase (DPD) Deficiency
* DPD is the primary catabolic enzyme for 5-FU.
* Deficiency leads to drug accumulation.
* Causes severe myelosuppression, neurotoxicity, and GI distress.

category: g
front: The outermost layer of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa, primarily synthesizes the mineralocorticoid [___].
back:
• Aldosterone
• Regulates salt and water metabolism
• Controlled by the renin-angiotensin system

category: g
front: A patient with Addison's disease is on hydrocortisone but remains hypotensive with persistent hyponatremia. The most appropriate pharmacological addition is [___].
back:
• Fludrocortisone
• Potent synthetic mineralocorticoid
• Corrects electrolyte imbalance and fluid status

category: g
front: Explain the mechanism by which glucocorticoids decrease the production of prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
back:
• Inhibits Phospholipase A2
• Prevents release of arachidonic acid
• Blocks the precursor for inflammatory mediators

category: g
front: Contrast the anti-inflammatory potency and salt-retaining activity of Dexamethasone compared to Hydrocortisone.
back:
• Dexamethasone: ~30x potency; zero salt retention
• Hydrocortisone: 1:1 ratio (standard reference)
• Dexamethasone preferred for cerebral edema

category: g
front: Identify the therapeutic rationale for intramuscular administration of betamethasone to a mother in preterm labor at 31 weeks gestation.
back:
• Accelerates fetal lung maturation
• Stimulates surfactant production
• Prevents neonatal respiratory distress syndrome

category: g
front: In the diagnosis of Cushing syndrome, the synthetic glucocorticoid [___] is used because it fails to suppress cortisol in hypercortisolism patients.
back:
• Dexamethasone
• Used in the Suppression Test
• Distinguishes true Cushing's from normal feedback

category: g
front: A patient on chronic high-dose prednisone for asthma abruptly stops medication. Predict the immediate clinical consequence.
back:
• Acute Adrenal Insufficiency (Crisis)
• Caused by HPA-axis suppression
• Risk of fatal cardiovascular collapse

category: g
front: Describe the biochemical target of Metyrapone and its effect on steroid precursors.
back:
• Inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase
• Blocks final cortisol synthesis step
• Causes accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol

category: g
front: Distinguish between Spironolactone and Eplerenone regarding their incidence of endocrine-related side effects.
back:
• Spironolactone: High (gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities)
• Eplerenone: Low (highly selective mineralocorticoid blocker)
• Both cause hyperkalemia

category: g
front: Identify the primary cellular location of inactive glucocorticoid receptors before binding to a ligand.
back:
• Cytoplasm (Cytosol)
• Complexed with heat-shock proteins (HSP90)
• Translocates to nucleus after dimerization

category: g
front: The outer layer of the adrenal cortex, known as the zona glomerulosa, primarily synthesizes the mineralocorticoid [___].
back: - Aldosterone. - Regulated by the renin-angiotensin system. - Controls salt and water metabolism. - Increases sodium reabsorption and potassium/hydrogen excretion.

category: g
front: A patient with hypotension and hyperpigmentation fails to respond to ACTH administration. Identify the pharmaceutical agent of choice for replacement and its diurnal dosing strategy.
back: - Hydrocortisone (identical to natural cortisol). - Administered in a 2:1 ratio (two-thirds morning, one-third afternoon). - Goal is to mimic normal diurnal variation. - Essential to prevent fatal acute adrenal insufficiency.

category: g
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which glucocorticoids inhibit the production of prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
back: - Inhibition of Phospholipase A2. - Blocks the release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids. - Leads to decreased synthesis of inflammatory mediators. - Central to potent anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions.

category: g
front: Contrast the androgenic side effect profile of Spironolactone with Eplerenone in the management of heart failure.
back: - Spironolactone: Competes for androgen receptors; causes gynecomastia and menstrual irregularities. - Eplerenone: Highly selective for mineralocorticoid receptors. - Avoids anti-androgenic side effects due to its specific binding profile.

category: g
front: Define the clinical timing and goal of 'neoadjuvant' chemotherapy compared to standard 'adjuvant' therapy.
back: - Neoadjuvant: Administered prior to surgery to shrink the primary tumor. - Adjuvant: Given after surgery to eradicate occult micrometastases. - Both aim to improve long-term disease-free survival.

category: g
front: [___] is an antifungal agent utilized in Cushing syndrome because it strongly inhibits all gonadal and adrenal steroid hormone synthesis.
back: - Ketoconazole. - Inhibits cholesterol side-chain cleavage and other P450 enzymes. - Used as a non-surgical treatment for hypercortisolism. - Requires close monitoring for potential hepatotoxicity.

category: g
front: A female infant presents with virilization due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. State the pharmacological objective of providing glucocorticoid therapy in this condition.
back: - Suppresses hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH release. - Restores negative feedback inhibition. - Reduces the overproduction of adrenal androgens. - Normalizes hormone levels to prevent further virilization.

category: g
front: Describe how the kidney prevents natural cortisol from activating mineralocorticoid receptors despite its high affinity for them.
back: - Expression of 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2. - Converts cortisol to its inactive 11-keto derivative (cortisone). - Cortisone has minimal action on aldosterone receptors. - Ensures receptor specificity in excretory organs.

category: g
front: Distinguish between Hydrocortisone and Dexamethasone regarding their relative anti-inflammatory potency and salt-retaining activity.
back: - Hydrocortisone: Potency 1; High salt retention (ratio 1:1). - Dexamethasone: Potency 30; Zero salt-retaining activity. - Dexamethasone is preferred for accelerating fetal lung maturation.

category: g
front: Explain the 'log-kill' hypothesis regarding the destruction of cancer cells by chemotherapeutic agents.
back: - Destruction follows first-order kinetics. - A constant fraction of cells is killed per dose, not a constant number. - 5-log kill reduces 10 to the 9th cells to 10 to the 4th cells. - Requires intermittent cycles to eradicate the total burden.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: The antimetabolite [___] is frequently utilized as a potent radiosensitizer in combined modality therapy for pancreatic and non-small cell lung cancers.
back:
* Gemcitabine
* It is a fluorine-substituted deoxycytidine analog
* Inhibits ribonucleotide reductase to deplete nucleotide pools

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with squamous cell carcinoma of the anus is starting concurrent chemoradiation. Which drug is specifically selected for this regimen because it targets hypoxic tumor stem cells that are typically resistant to radiation?
back:
* Mitomycin (Mitomycin C)
* Acts as a bioreductive alkylating agent
* Synergizes with radiation by attacking cells in low-oxygen environments

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Explain the biochemical synergy achieved when Cisplatin is administered during the radiotherapy phase of cancer treatment.
back:
* Inhibits the repair of radiation-induced DNA lesions
* Forms intrastrand and interstrand DNA cross-links
* Synchronizes cells into radiosensitive phases of the cell cycle

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A 60-year-old patient with newly diagnosed glioblastoma multiforme is prescribed a daily oral alkylating agent to be taken concurrently with cranial radiation. Identify the drug and its primary physiological advantage in this setting.
back:
* Temozolomide
* Exhibits excellent blood-brain barrier penetration
* Methylates DNA and inhibits the repair enzyme O6-guanine-DNA alkyltransferase

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Identify the primary therapeutic goal of administering 'neoadjuvant' chemotherapy prior to the initiation of definitive radiotherapy.
back:
* Reduce the volume of the primary tumor (debulking)
* Improve the technical feasibility of subsequent local therapy
* Eradicate early micrometastases

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: Cetuximab in Head and Neck Radiotherapy
front: In patients with locally advanced head and neck cancer, the monoclonal antibody [___] is often combined with radiotherapy to enhance the inhibition of downstream growth signaling.
back:
* Cetuximab
* Targets the extracellular domain of the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)
* Interferes with DNA repair and promotes apoptosis

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: A patient with rectal cancer is receiving a 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) infusion alongside pelvic radiation. How does this 'radiosensitization' specifically target the S-phase of the tumor cell cycle?
back:
* Depletes thymidine through thymidylate synthase (TS) inhibition
* Creates an 'imbalanced growth' state making DNA more vulnerable to radiation
* Incorporates fluorinated nucleotides into RNA/DNA

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Contrast the clinical use of Bevacizumab versus Cetuximab when utilized in conjunction with local radiation therapies.
back:
* Bevacizumab: Targets VEGF-A to inhibit tumor angiogenesis and neovascularization.
* Cetuximab: Targets EGFR to inhibit cellular proliferation and invasion.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
front: Distinguish between the radiosensitizing mechanisms of Taxanes (e.g., Paclitaxel) and Antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU) regarding cell cycle arrest.
back:
* Taxanes: Arrest cells in the M-phase (the most radiosensitive phase) by stabilizing microtubules.
* Antimetabolites: Primarily target the S-phase by interfering with DNA synthesis and repair.

category: Explain the drugs used during phases of radiotherapy, e
coreConcept: Combined Modality Therapy for Anal Cancer
front: Name the specific drug utilized during the treatment of locally advanced anal cancer to enhance the effects of radiotherapy while allowing for organ-sparing (rectal preservation).
back:
* Mitomycin C (often combined with 5-FU)
* Highly effective in attacking the core of solid tumors
* Reduces the need for radical surgery

category: g
front: The primary zone of the adrenal cortex responsible for the synthesis and secretion of mineralocorticoids, such as aldosterone, is the [___].
back:
• Zona glomerulosa (outermost layer)
• Synthesizes aldosterone from cholesterol
• Primarily regulated by the renin-angiotensin system and potassium levels

category: g
front: A 35-year-old female with primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) remains hyponatremic despite hydrocortisone therapy. Identify the most appropriate pharmacological addition to her regimen.
back:
• Fludrocortisone
• Provides potent salt-retaining (mineralocorticoid) activity
• Essential for correcting electrolyte imbalances in primary, but not always secondary, insufficiency

category: g
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which glucocorticoids exert their potent anti-inflammatory effects regarding arachidonic acid metabolites.
back:
• Induction of lipocortins (annexins)
• Direct inhibition of Phospholipase A2
• Prevents release of arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, blocking both prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis

category: g
front: Contrast the pharmacological specificity and clinical adverse effects of spironolactone versus eplerenone in the management of hyperaldosteronism.
back:
• Spironolactone: Non-selective; antagonizes both mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors (causes gynecomastia/hirsutism)
• Eplerenone: Highly selective mineralocorticoid antagonist
• Eplerenone significantly lacks the endocrine side effects associated with spironolactone

category: g
front: Describe the physiological basis of the Dexamethasone Suppression Test in diagnosing hypercortisolism.
back:
• Utilizes negative feedback mechanism
• Dexamethasone suppresses ACTH and cortisol in normal individuals
• Lack of suppression suggests autonomous production (Cushing Syndrome)

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The tumor suppressor protein that halts the cell cycle at the G1/S transition by sequestering the E2F transcription factor is [___].
back:
*   Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein.
*   Active when hypophosphorylated.
*   Prevents transcription of S-phase genes.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A biopsy of a rapidly growing lung carcinoma reveals a loss-of-function mutation in a gene that normally induces p21 to inhibit Cyclin-CDK complexes in response to DNA damage. This finding characterizes a failure of which checkpoint?
back:
*   G1/S Checkpoint.
*   Mediated by p53.
*   Loss leads to replication of damaged DNA.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) are activated to drive cell cycle progression.
back:
*   Binding of regulatory Cyclin proteins.
*   Phosphorylation of the T-loop by CDK-activating kinase (CAK).
*   Removal of inhibitory phosphates.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the mutations typically seen in proto-oncogenes versus tumor suppressor genes in the context of oncogenic transformation.
back:
*   Proto-oncogenes: Gain-of-function mutations; require only one allele (dominant).
*   Tumor Suppressors: Loss-of-function mutations; usually require both alleles (recessive/two-hit).

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Outline the specific role of the p21 protein in maintaining genomic stability after exposure to ionizing radiation.
back:
*   CDK inhibitor (CKI).
*   Transcribed by p53.
*   Inhibits Cyclin E/CDK2 and Cyclin D/CDK4/6 to cause G1 arrest.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The checkpoint that prevents chromosome missegregation by ensuring all kinetochores are properly attached to spindle fibers is the [___] checkpoint.
back:
*   M-phase (Spindle Assembly) checkpoint.
*   Prevents transition to anaphase.
*   Involves the Anaphase-Promoting Complex (APC).

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A young patient presenting with multiple primary malignancies (sarcoma and breast cancer) likely possesses a germline mutation in a gene that normally senses DNA stress. Identify the gene and its primary tumor-suppressive action.
back:
*   TP53 (Li-Fraumeni Syndrome).
*   Upregulates BAX/PUMA for apoptosis.
*   Upregulates p21 for cell cycle arrest.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe the molecular interaction involving Cyclin D and CDK4/6 that specifically triggers the 'Restriction Point' bypass.
back:
*   Cyclin D/CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb.
*   Rb releases E2F.
*   E2F activates transcription of Cyclin E and S-phase machinery.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints based on the primary internal stimulus that triggers arrest.
back:
*   G1/S Checkpoint: DNA damage and environmental mitogens.
*   G2/M Checkpoint: Completion of DNA replication and replication errors.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe how growth factor signaling influences the accumulation of the specific cyclin required to initiate the cell cycle from the G0 phase.
back:
*   Induces Cyclin D synthesis.
*   Activates Ras/MAPK pathway.
*   Cyclin D levels rise to bind CDK4/6.

category: g
front: Glucocorticoids exert potent anti-inflammatory effects by inducing lipocortins, which directly inhibit the enzyme [___], thereby blocking the liberation of arachidonic acid from cell membranes.
back:
* Phospholipase A2 (PLA2)
* Prevents synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes
* Reduces the overall inflammatory precursor pool

category: g
front: A 19-year-old male presents with anorexia, postural hypotension, and skin hyperpigmentation. Laboratory analysis reveals hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. These electrolyte abnormalities are primarily caused by a deficiency in which specific hormone?
back:
* Aldosterone
* Leads to decreased sodium reabsorption and impaired potassium/H+ excretion
* Common in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)

category: g
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism that allows the kidney to maintain mineralocorticoid receptor specificity for aldosterone despite high circulating levels of cortisol.
back:
* Expression of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2
* Converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone
* Prevents cortisol from overwhelming mineralocorticoid receptors in the distal tubule

category: g
front: Contrast the hormonal profile and the diagnostic response to exogenous ACTH in a patient with pituitary-driven secondary adrenal insufficiency versus one with autoimmune-driven primary adrenal insufficiency.
back:
* Primary: High ACTH, low cortisol; no response to exogenous ACTH.
* Secondary: Low ACTH, low cortisol; cortisol levels rise after ACTH administration.
* Mineralocorticoids are largely preserved in secondary insufficiency (controlled by RAAS).

category: g
front: Describe the pharmacological rationale for preferring Prednisone in pregnant women needing systemic corticosteroid therapy to minimize fetal drug exposure.
back:
* Prednisone is a prodrug; the fetal liver cannot convert it to active prednisolone
* Maternal prednisolone is converted back to inactive prednisone by placental 11β-HSD type 2
* Protects the fetus from active glucocorticoid effects

category: g
front: In the differential diagnosis of Cushing syndrome, the synthetic glucocorticoid used to demonstrate a failure of negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is [___].
back:
* Dexamethasone
* Used in the Dexamethasone Suppression Test
* Distinguishes between normal HPA function and hypercortisolism

category: g
front: A female neonate with ambiguous genitalia and 21β-hydroxylase deficiency is started on Hydrocortisone. Explain the primary physiological goal of this replacement therapy regarding adrenal androgen production.
back:
* Provides negative feedback to the hypothalamus and pituitary
* Suppresses excessive ACTH secretion
* Reduces the drive for adrenal androgen precursor accumulation and virilization

category: g
front: A patient with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction develops painful gynecomastia while on an aldosterone antagonist. Explain the mechanism of this side effect and suggest a more selective alternative from the same class.
back:
* Mechanism: Spironolactone non-selectively antagonizes androgen receptors.
* Alternative: Eplerenone.
* Eplerenone specifically binds the mineralocorticoid receptor with minimal androgen receptor affinity.

category: g
front: Contrast the acute effect of high-dose glucocorticoid administration on circulating neutrophil counts versus lymphocyte and eosinophil counts.
back:
* Neutrophils: Increased count (due to demargination and marrow release).
* Lymphocytes/Eosinophils: Decreased count (due to redistribution to lymphoid tissue).
* Rapid change in leukocyte profile following administration.

category: g
coreConcept: Functional Anatomy of the Adrenal Cortex
front: Identify the three distinct zones of the adrenal cortex and the primary corticosteroid class produced by each, moving from the outer capsule to the inner medulla.
back:
* Zona Glomerulosa: Mineralocorticoids (Aldosterone)
* Zona Fasciculata: Glucocorticoids (Cortisol)
* Zona Reticularis: Adrenal Androgens (DHEA)

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The 'guardian of the genome' that induces cell cycle arrest in the G1 phase to allow for DNA repair before replication is [___].
back:
• p53 protein
• Acts as a transcription factor for p21
• Inhibits Cyclin-CDK complexes
• Triggers apoptosis if DNA damage is irreversible

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
coreConcept: Li-Fraumeni Syndrome and Cell Cycle Arrest
front: A 25-year-old patient presents with a family history of diverse early-onset malignancies including sarcomas and breast cancer. Dysregulation of which cell cycle regulator is most likely?
back:
• p53 (Li-Fraumeni Syndrome)
• Loss of G1/S checkpoint control
• Leads to accumulation of mutations
• Promotes survival of genetically unstable cells

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which the Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein prevents premature entry into the S-phase.
back:
• Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F transcription factors
• Prevents transcription of S-phase genes
• CDK4/6-Cyclin D phosphorylates Rb to release E2F
• Loss of Rb leads to constitutive S-phase entry

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the genetic 'drivers' of oncogenesis by distinguishing the required mutations in proto-oncogenes versus tumor suppressor genes.
back:
• Proto-oncogenes: Gain-of-function (one allele enough)
• Tumor Suppressors: Loss-of-function (both alleles; Knudson's 'Two-Hit')
• Oncogenes promote cycle progression
• Suppressors inhibit cycle progression

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe the consequence of Cyclin D1 overexpression in the context of the cellular growth cycle.
back:
• Accelerates G1 to S phase transition
• Overcomes normal inhibitory signals
• Commonly seen in mantle cell lymphoma
• Persistent phosphorylation of Rb protein

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Mature, non-dividing cells that have exited the cell cycle but remain metabolically active are in the [___] phase.
back:
• G0 (Quiescent) phase
• Can re-enter cycle via growth factors
• Stem cells reside here frequently
• Malignant cells often fail to enter this phase

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A child presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). Histology shows Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Which molecular 'brake' of the cell cycle is dysfunctional?
back:
• Rb Protein (Retinoblastoma)
• Found on Chromosome 13q14
• Regulates the G1-S transition point
• Uncontrolled E2F activation drives proliferation

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: How does the overexpression of Bcl-2 contribute to oncogenesis if it does not directly speed up the cell cycle?
back:
• Inhibits apoptosis (anti-apoptotic)
• Allows cells with damaged DNA to survive
• Provides time for further oncogenic mutations
• Common in Follicular Lymphoma (t:14,18)

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the primary purpose of the G1/S checkpoint versus the G2/M checkpoint.
back:
• G1/S: Checks for DNA damage before replication
• G2/M: Checks for unduplicated DNA/errors after replication
• G1/S involves p53/p21/Rb
• G2/M prevents entry into mitosis with errors

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Define the role of Cyclin-Dependent Kinase Inhibitors (CDKIs) like p16 and p21 in a healthy cell.
back:
• Act as tumor suppressors
• Inactivate CDK-Cyclin complexes
• Halt cycle to allow DNA repair
• p16 often deleted in various carcinomas

category: g
front: The drug [___] is a potent synthetic mineralocorticoid with some glucocorticoid activity, used primarily to supplement electrolyte and salt regulation in patients with primary adrenocortical insufficiency.
back: Fludrocortisone. • Corrects hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in Addison's disease. • Promotes renal sodium reabsorption. • Used when hydrocortisone alone is insufficient for fluid status control.

category: g
front: A patient with Cushing's syndrome is treated with an antifungal agent that inhibits multiple cytochrome P450 enzymes, including the cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme. Name this drug and its primary endocrine risk.
back: Ketoconazole. • Non-selective inhibitor of all adrenal and gonadal steroidogenesis. • Can induce acute adrenal insufficiency. • Also acts as an androgen antagonist, potentially causing gynecomastia.

category: g
front: Outline the molecular mechanism by which glucocorticoids exert their potent anti-inflammatory effects through the inhibition of Phospholipase A2.
back: Annexin-1 (Lipocortin) Induction. • Glucocorticoids bind intracellular receptors to modulate gene transcription. • Increases annexin-1 production. • Directly inhibits Phospholipase A2, preventing the release of arachidonic acid and subsequent eicosanoids.

category: g
front: Contrast the specific microtubule dynamics affected by Vinca alkaloids versus Taxanes during the mitotic phase of the cell cycle.
back: Polymerization vs. Depolymerization. • Vincas (e.g., Vincristine): Bind tubulin to inhibit polymerization, preventing spindle assembly. • Taxanes (e.g., Paclitaxel): Stabilize microtubules to prevent depolymerization/disassembly. • Both result in M-phase mitotic arrest.

category: g
front: Identify the standard cytoprotectant administered alongside high-dose cyclophosphamide to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis and describe its chemical interaction.
back: Mesna (Sodium 2-mercaptoethane sulfonate). • Administered to neutralize acrolein in the bladder. • Binds chemically to the toxic metabolite acrolein. • Prevents irritation and subsequent fibrosis of the bladder wall.

category: g
front: The antimetabolite [___] is an oral prodrug that undergoes a triple-step enzymatic conversion, finishing with thymidine phosphorylase, to be converted into the active agent 5-fluorouracil within tumor cells.
back: Capecitabine. • Selective for tumor tissues expressing high thymidine phosphorylase. • Inhibits thymidylate synthase. • Commonly used for metastatic colorectal and breast cancers.

category: g
front: A 50-year-old male treated for colorectal cancer presents with painful erythema on his palms and soles, plus a unique neuropathy triggered by exposure to cold liquids. Which drug in his regimen is responsible?
back: Oxaliplatin. • Platinum analog associated with cold-induced peripheral sensory neuropathy. • Can also cause hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia). • Core component of the FOLFOX chemotherapy regimen.

category: g
front: Explain the molecular pathway by which Trastuzumab (Herceptin) induces cytotoxicity in HER2-overexpressing breast cancer cells.
back: HER2 Signaling Blockade. • Binds the extracellular domain of the HER2 growth receptor. • Inhibits intracellular tyrosine kinase signaling. • Induces antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and reduces cells in the S-phase.

category: g
front: Contrast the receptor selectivity and subsequent side effect profiles of Spironolactone versus Eplerenone in the treatment of hyperaldosteronism.
back: Selective vs. Non-selective Antagonism. • Spironolactone: Non-selective; antagonizes androgen and progesterone receptors, causing gynecomastia. • Eplerenone: Highly selective for mineralocorticoid receptors. • Eplerenone lacks the hormonal side effects of spironolactone.

category: g
front: State the specific clinical indication for administering Dexamethasone or Betamethasone to a mother within 48 hours of anticipated premature delivery.
back: Acceleration of Fetal Lung Maturation. • Stimulates the production of fetal pulmonary surfactant. • Prevents neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS). • These drugs are chosen because they cross the placenta readily.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The critical tumor suppressor protein that acts as the 'Governor of the Cell Cycle' by inhibiting the G1 to S phase transition through E2F binding is [___].
back:
• Retinoblastoma protein (Rb).
• Prevents entry into S-phase when hypophosphorylated.
• Released upon phosphorylation by Cyclin D-CDK4/6.
• Loss of function leads to uncontrolled proliferation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A biopsy of a rapidly growing lung mass reveals a mutation in the TP53 gene. In response to DNA damage, this protein normally induces cell cycle arrest by transcriptionally activating [___].
back:
• p21 (a CKI).
• p21 inhibits Cyclin-CDK complexes.
• Maintains Rb in hypophosphorylated state.
• Halts the cell cycle to allow DNA repair or triggers apoptosis.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the biological role of Cyclin-Dependent Kinase Inhibitors (CKIs) such as p16 in maintaining cellular homeostasis.
back:
• Competitively bind to CDKs.
• Block phosphorylation of the Rb protein.
• Enforce the G1 restriction point.
• Act as tumor suppressors; their loss allows premature S-phase entry.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A patient's tumor exhibits MYC amplification while another shows PTEN deletion. Contrast the oncogenic mechanisms of transcription factor overexpression versus loss of phosphatase activity.
back:
• MYC: Direct transcriptional activation of pro-growth genes like Cyclins.
• PTEN loss: Failure to inhibit the PI3K/AKT pro-survival pathway.
• Both result in constitutive signaling and metabolic reprogramming.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Outline the 'Two-Hit' hypothesis as it applies to the inactivation of tumor suppressor genes in hereditary versus sporadic cancers.
back:
• Hereditary: One germline mutation inherited; second hit acquired somatically.
• Sporadic: Both alleles inactivated via independent somatic mutations.
• Explains the earlier onset of familial cancer syndromes.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The point in the cell cycle where the cell becomes committed to division, regardless of extracellular growth factors, is known as the [___].
back:
• Restriction (R) point.
• Located in late G1 phase.
• Regulated primarily by the Rb/E2F pathway.
• Beyond this, the cell completes the cycle autonomously.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Molecular analysis of a Burkitt Lymphoma specimen shows an 8;14 translocation. This chromosomal abnormality results in oncogenesis by placing the [___] gene under the control of the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
back:
• MYC oncogene.
• Leads to constitutive MYC protein expression.
• Drives continuous transition into S-phase.
• Promotes rapid, autonomous B-cell proliferation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Detail the sequence of events at the G2/M checkpoint that prevents a cell with unrepaired DNA damage from entering mitosis.
back:
• DNA damage sensors activate kinases (ATM/ATR).
• Inactivation of Cdc25 phosphatase occurs.
• Prevents activation of the Cyclin B-CDK1 complex.
• Arrests cell in G2 to maintain genomic stability.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between Proto-oncogenes and Tumor Suppressor Genes regarding their normal function and the nature of mutations that lead to cancer.
back:
• Proto-oncogenes: Promote growth; require gain-of-function (dominant) mutations.
• Tumor Suppressors: Inhibit growth/repair DNA; require loss-of-function (recessive) mutations.
• Cancer arises from the imbalance of these signals.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the primary cyclin-CDK complex responsible for driving the cell past the G1/S transition.
back:
• Cyclin E-CDK2.
• Phosphorylates Rb to finalize E2F release.
• Initiates DNA polymerase activity.
• Essential for successful entry into the S (synthesis) phase.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The 'guardian of the genome,' [___], prevents oncogenesis by inducing cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage.
back:
● p53 protein
● Acts at the G1/S checkpoint
● Allows time for DNA repair
● Triggers programmed cell death if damage is irreversible, preventing the propagation of mutations.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 2-year-old child presents with a white pupillary reflex. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in a protein that normally inhibits E2F. Name the protein and the specific cell cycle transition it regulates.
back:
● Rb (Retinoblastoma) protein
● Regulates the G1 to S phase transition
● In its hypophosphorylated state, it binds E2F to stop progression
● Loss of function leads to autonomous entry into the S phase.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the role of Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) in the progression of the cell cycle toward malignancy.
back:
● CDKs are enzymes activated by cyclins
● They phosphorylate target proteins to drive cycle phases
● Overexpression of CDKs or cyclins causes bypass of regulatory checkpoints
● Results in uncontrolled cellular proliferation and tumor formation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the 'gain-of-function' mutations in proto-oncogenes with 'loss-of-function' mutations in tumor suppressor genes regarding cell cycle impact.
back:
● Proto-oncogenes: One mutated allele (dominant) causes constitutive cycle stimulation (e.g., RAS)
● Tumor Suppressors: Both alleles must be inactivated (recessive) to lose cycle inhibition (e.g., p53, Rb)
● Both lead to unregulated growth.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
