front: How do tumor cells in the G0 phase contribute to chemotherapy resistance and cancer recurrence?
back:
● G0 is a quiescent/resting state
● Cell Cycle Specific (CCS) drugs target actively dividing cells (e.g., S or M phase)
● G0 cells survive treatment and can re-enter the cycle later, causing relapse.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The primary checkpoint that monitors whether DNA replication is complete and checks for DNA damage before entering mitosis is the [___] checkpoint.
back:
● G2/M checkpoint
● Prevents the cell from dividing with damaged or incomplete DNA
● Failure at this stage leads to mitotic catastrophe or genomic instability in daughter cells.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A patient with multiple primary cancers at a young age is diagnosed with Li-Fraumeni Syndrome. This condition involves a germline mutation affecting which regulatory process?
back:
● TP53 gene mutation
● Affects the G1/S DNA damage checkpoint
● Loss of p53 means the cell cannot halt for repair before DNA synthesis
● Results in a high frequency of diverse malignancies.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe how a defect in the M-phase spindle assembly checkpoint contributes to aneuploidy in oncogenesis.
back:
● Failure to ensure all chromosomes are attached to spindle fibers
● Results in unequal distribution of chromatids during anaphase
● Leads to daughter cells with abnormal chromosome numbers (aneuploidy)
● Promotes further genetic instability.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between quiescence and senescence in the context of the cell cycle and malignancy.
back:
● Quiescence (G0): Reversible resting state; cells can re-enter cycle under growth factor stimulation
● Senescence: Irreversible exit from the cycle
● Senescence acts as a protective mechanism against telomere shortening or oncogene activation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the critical enzyme that helps cancer cells bypass the 'Hayflick limit' of the cell cycle to achieve immortality.
back:
● Telomerase
● Maintains telomere length at chromosome ends
● Most somatic cells lack this, leading to senescence
● 90% of human cancers upregulate telomerase to achieve limitless replicative potential.

category: g
front: The outer layer of the adrenal cortex, known as the [___], is the primary site for mineralocorticoid synthesis under the regulation of the renin-angiotensin system.
back:
• Zona glomerulosa
• Primary site for mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) synthesis from cholesterol
• Regulates salt and water balance through renal sodium reabsorption
• Secretion is primarily controlled by Angiotensin II and serum potassium

category: g
front: A 40-year-old female on chronic high-dose prednisone for rheumatoid arthritis presents with hypotension and lethargy after abrupt medication cessation. This crisis occurs because [___].
back:
• Acute Adrenal Insufficiency (Adrenal Crisis)
• Prolonged prednisone use suppresses the HPA axis
• Results in adrenal cortical atrophy and low cortisol reserve
• Abrupt cessation prevents the body from mounting a stress response

category: g
front: Detail the intracellular metabolic transformation and enzymatic target required for 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) to inhibit DNA synthesis.
back:
• Metabolic conversion to the active 5-FdUMP
• Covalently binds and inhibits the enzyme thymidylate synthase
• Requires reduced folate (leucovorin) to form a stable complex
• Resulting thymineless death blocks DNA synthesis in S-phase

category: g
front: Compare the expected dose-limiting toxicities in two oncology patients: one receiving Vincristine for lymphoma and the other receiving Vinblastine for testicular cancer.
back:
• Vincristine: Dose-limiting neurotoxicity (paresthesias, ataxia, constipation)
• Vinblastine: Dose-limiting myelosuppression (leukopenia and bone marrow suppression)
• Both disrupt microtubule polymerization in the M-phase
• Vincristine is often used when bone marrow must be spared

category: g
front: Predict the outcome of a dexamethasone suppression test in a patient with iatrogenic Cushing syndrome compared to an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor.
back:
• Iatrogenic Cushing: ACTH and cortisol suppression occurs due to feedback
• Pituitary Tumor (Cushing Disease): Suppresses only with high-dose dexamethasone
• Ectopic ACTH Tumor: Fails to suppress even with high-dose dexamethasone
• Helps differentiate etiologies of hypercortisolism

category: g
front: Patients receiving [___] must be monitored via pulmonary function tests due to the risk of dose-dependent, potentially fatal interstitial fibrosis.
back:
• Bleomycin (Antitumor antibiotic)
• Generates oxygen free radicals leading to single/double-strand DNA scissions
• Target tissues (lung/skin) lack the inactivating enzyme bleomycin hydrolase
• Leads to pulmonary pneumonitis and potentially fatal interstitial fibrosis

category: g
front: An infant with ambiguous genitalia and salt-wasting is diagnosed with 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Explain the rationale for administering hydrocortisone in this condition.
back:
• Inhibits elevated secretion of CRH and ACTH via negative feedback
• Diverts adrenal steroid precursors away from the androgenic pathway
• Restores normal glucocorticoid levels and suppresses further female virilization
• Normalization of growth and bone maturation is a primary goal

category: g
front: Elucidate the specific enzymatic blockade by which corticosteroids prevent the release of arachidonic acid from cell membranes during inflammation.
back:
• Promotes the synthesis of Annexin-1 (lipocortin)
• Annexin-1 directly inhibits the Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) enzyme
• Prevents the release of arachidonic acid from cellular membranes
• Blocks synthesis of both prostaglandins (COX) and leukotrienes (LOX)

category: g
front: Differentiate between hydrocortisone and dexamethasone based on their relative anti-inflammatory versus salt-retaining (mineralocorticoid) potencies.
back:
• Hydrocortisone: 1:1 ratio (significant anti-inflammatory and mineralocorticoid activity)
• Dexamethasone: 30:0 ratio (potent anti-inflammatory effect with zero salt retention)
• Hydrocortisone: Short-acting agent used for physiological adrenal replacement
• Dexamethasone: Long-acting agent used for severe systemic inflammation

category: g
front: Identify the principle of chemotherapy which states that a constant fraction of tumor cells is killed with each treatment cycle regardless of the total burden.
back:
• The Log-kill Hypothesis
• Anti-cancer drugs follow first-order kinetics (percentage reduction per dose)
• Fixed fraction of cells is killed regardless of the tumor burden
• Implies that multiple treatment cycles are necessary to achieve cure

category: g
front: The outer layer of the adrenal cortex, the zona glomerulosa, primarily synthesizes the mineralocorticoid [___].
back: * Aldosterone * Regulates sodium and water retention * Controlled primarily by the renin-angiotensin system

category: g
front: A patient with primary adrenocortical insufficiency presents with hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes. Identify the precursor molecule responsible for this finding.
back: * Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) * Cleaved into ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) * Elevated due to the loss of negative feedback from cortisol

category: g
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which glucocorticoids achieve their potent anti-inflammatory effects by targeting membrane lipid metabolism.
back: * Inhibition of Phospholipase A2 * Prevents the release of arachidonic acid * Blocks the production of both prostaglandins and leukotrienes

category: g
front: Contrast the receptor specificity and side effect profile of Spironolactone versus Eplerenone in the management of heart failure.
back: * Spironolactone: Non-selective (antagonizes androgen and progesterone receptors); causes gynecomastia. * Eplerenone: Highly selective mineralocorticoid antagonist. * Both: Induce hyperkalemia.

category: g
front: State the rationale for administering Mesna as a cytoprotectant during high-dose Ifosfamide or Cyclophosphamide therapy.
back: * Binds and neutralizes acrolein in the urine * Prevents hemorrhagic cystitis * Concentrates in the bladder to protect the urothelium

category: g
front: In the diagnostic workup of Cushing syndrome, the [___] suppression test is utilized to distinguish between normal pituitary function and autonomous cortisol production.
back: * Dexamethasone * Evaluates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis * Failure of suppression indicates pathological hypercortisolism

category: g
front: A patient treated with Doxorubicin develops signs of congestive heart failure. Identify the cellular mechanism of this injury and the recommended protective agent.
back: * Generation of oxygen free radicals * Causes irreversible dose-dependent dilated cardiomyopathy * Dexrazoxane is the protective iron-chelating agent

category: g
front: Describe the specific mechanism of action for Trastuzumab and the biological requirement for its clinical efficacy in breast cancer management.
back: * Binds to the extracellular domain of the HER2 receptor * Inhibits downstream proliferative tyrosine kinase signaling * Requires confirmation of tumor HER2/neu overexpression

category: g
front: Distinguish between the primary dose-limiting toxicities of the Vinca alkaloids Vincristine and Vinblastine.
back: * Vincristine: Neurotoxicity (peripheral neuropathy and constipation) * Vinblastine: Bone marrow suppression (myelosuppression) * Both: Interfere with microtubule polymerization

category: g
front: Identify the principal human glucocorticoid produced in the middle layer (zona fasciculata) of the adrenal cortex.
back: * Cortisol * Regulates intermediary metabolism and stress response * Promotes gluconeogenesis and protein catabolism

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The tumor suppressor gene frequently mutated in over 50% of human solid tumors, which normally functions to monitor DNA integrity at cell cycle checkpoints, is [___].
back: p53 (TP53). * Functions as a transcription factor. * Triggers DNA repair or apoptosis. * Prevents replication of damaged DNA.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
coreConcept: Rb Gene and Cell Cycle Regulation
front: A child presents with a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria). Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in a gene that normally inhibits the G1 to S phase transition by binding to the E2F transcription factor. This gene is [___].
back: Rb (Retinoblastoma) gene. * Normally inhibits G1-S transition. * Phosphorylation by CDK4/6 releases E2F. * Loss causes unregulated cell cycle entry.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain how proto-oncogenes contribute to oncogenesis when they become mutated into oncogenes.
back: * Proto-oncogenes normally promote growth. * Mutations create 'gain-of-function' oncogenes. * Leads to constitutive signaling (e.g., mutated Ras or ErbB receptors).

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the efficacy of Cell Cycle-Specific (CCS) drugs versus Cell Cycle-Nonspecific (CCNS) drugs based on a tumor's growth fraction.
back: * CCS drugs target specific phases; effective in high-growth-fraction tumors. * CCNS drugs (e.g., alkylating agents) kill cycling and G0 cells. * CCNS are crucial for debulking solid tumors.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Define the term 'Growth Fraction' in the context of tumor susceptibility to chemotherapy.
back: * The percentage of tumor cells actively dividing. * Determines chemotherapy sensitivity. * High growth fraction correlates with better response to Cell Cycle-Specific drugs.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Chemotherapeutic agents like Antimetabolites (e.g., Methotrexate, 5-FU) specifically exert their cytotoxic effects during the [___] phase of the cell cycle.
back: S phase. * Period of DNA replication. * Antimetabolites interfere with nucleotide synthesis or incorporation. * Specificity limits damage to non-dividing normal cells.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A biopsy of a lung adenocarcinoma shows a loss-of-function mutation in the p53 gene. Describe the expected cellular response to chemotherapy-induced DNA damage in this patient.
back: * Impaired cell cycle arrest. * Defective apoptosis despite DNA damage. * Accumulation of further mutations. * Clinically manifests as poor response to DNA-damaging drugs.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: How does the Gompertzian model of tumor growth explain why large solid tumors are often less responsive to chemotherapy?
back: * Growth rate slows as tumor size increases. * Large tumors have many cells in G0 (resting phase). * CCS drugs cannot kill non-cycling cells. * Result: Reduced log-kill.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between the genetic requirements for oncogenesis involving tumor suppressor genes versus proto-oncogenes.
back: * Proto-oncogenes: One 'hit' (gain-of-function) causes oncogenesis. * Tumor Suppressors: Two 'hits' (loss-of-function) usually required. * Reflects dominant vs. recessive cellular phenotypes.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the phase of the cell cycle inhibited by Vinca Alkaloids and Taxanes.
back: M phase (Mitosis). * Vinca alkaloids prevent spindle formation. * Taxanes prevent spindle breakdown. * Both cause mitotic arrest and subsequent apoptosis.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The critical tumor suppressor gene, often termed the 'guardian of the genome,' that triggers cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage is [___].
back:
● p53 protein
● Functions at the G1/S checkpoint
● Mutation allows replication of damaged DNA
● Found in >50% of human cancers

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 4-year-old boy presents with leukocoria (white pupillary reflex). Genetic testing confirms a biallelic mutation on chromosome 13. Describe the cellular mechanism leading to this malignancy.
back:
● Loss of Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein function
● Inability to sequester E2F transcription factor
● Uncontrolled transition from G1 to S phase
● Leads to Retinoblastoma

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the role of Cyclin-Dependent Kinase (CDK) overactivation in the development of malignancy.
back:
● CDKs drive the cell cycle forward
● Overactivation bypasses the G1/S restriction point
● Leads to persistent phosphorylation of Rb
● Results in autonomous, unregulated cell division

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the genetic 'hit' requirements for Proto-oncogenes versus Tumor Suppressor Genes to achieve oncogenic potential.
back:
● Proto-oncogenes: One 'hit' (gain-of-function/dominant)
● Tumor Suppressors: Two 'hits' (loss-of-function/recessive)
● Follows Knudson’s 'Two-Hit' hypothesis
● Results in loss of growth inhibition

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Detail the consequence of a mutation in the RAS protein regarding its GTPase activity in signaling pathways.
back:
● Loss of intrinsic GTPase activity
● RAS remains trapped in active GTP-bound state
● Continuous mitogenic signaling to the nucleus
● Drives cells into the S phase

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: In the cell cycle, the checkpoint that ensures all chromosomes are properly attached to the spindle before anaphase is the [___] checkpoint.
back:
● M (Spindle) checkpoint
● Prevents aneuploidy
● Monitored by APC/C complex
● Failure leads to chromosomal instability in tumors

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A patient is found to have a t(9;22) translocation resulting in a Bcr-Abl fusion protein. How does this specific abnormality drive leukemia?
back:
● Creates constitutive Tyrosine Kinase activity
● Bypasses normal growth factor requirements
● Activates pro-proliferative/anti-apoptotic pathways
● Pathognomonic for Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML)

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: How does the inhibition of the Mismatch Repair (MMR) pathway contribute to the stepwise progression of colorectal cancer?
back:
● Microsatellite instability (MSI)
● Accumulation of mutations in growth-regulating genes
● Failure to repair DNA replication errors
● Seen in Lynch Syndrome (HNPCC)

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between the G1/S and G2/M checkpoints based on the physiological errors they monitor.
back:
● G1/S: Checks for DNA damage and nutrients
● G2/M: Checks for DNA replication completion
● Both aim to prevent genomic mutation transfer
● Malignancy usually involves bypass of G1/S

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Define 'Growth Fraction' and explain why tumors with a high fraction are more susceptible to traditional chemotherapy.
back:
● Percentage of cells actively in the cell cycle
● Chemotherapy (CCS drugs) targets dividing cells
● High fraction equals rapid tumor doubling
● Examples: Burkitt Lymphoma, Leukemias

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Often termed the 'guardian of the genome,' the tumor suppressor protein that arrests the cell cycle in G1 upon detecting DNA damage is [___].
back:
p53 protein.
- Arrests cycle via p21 induction to allow DNA repair.
- Triggers apoptosis if damage is irreversible.
- Most frequently mutated gene in human cancers.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 25-year-old patient with a family history of early-onset sarcomas and breast cancer is found to have a germline mutation affecting p53. Identify the syndrome and its relation to the cell cycle.
back:
Li-Fraumeni Syndrome.
- Caused by germline TP53 mutations.
- Leads to loss of G1/S checkpoint control.
- Results in multiple primary malignancies due to unregulated division.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the role of the Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein in regulating the entry of a cell into the S-phase.
back:
- Hypophosphorylated Rb binds and sequesters E2F transcription factors.
- Prevents transition to S-phase.
- CDK4/6 phosphorylation releases E2F to trigger DNA synthesis genes.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A patient with cervical carcinoma has a biopsy revealing Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Specify how the viral E7 protein specifically disrupts cell cycle regulation.
back:
Inactivation of the Rb protein.
- E7 binds to Rb, releasing E2F transcription factors.
- Cell is forced into S-phase without normal growth signals.
- Overcomes the G1/S restriction point.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe the functional requirement of Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) to become active during the cell cycle.
back:
CDKs must bind to specific Cyclin regulatory subunits.
- Cyclin levels fluctuate; CDKs are constitutively expressed but inactive alone.
- Formation of the complex allows phosphorylation of target proteins (like Rb).

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The critical transition point where a cell becomes independent of external growth factors and commits to DNA replication is the [___] checkpoint.
back:
G1/S (Restriction) Checkpoint.
- Primary site of cell cycle regulation.
- Often bypassed in cancer via Cyclin D overexpression.
- Regulated by the Rb/E2F pathway.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A biopsy of a breast tumor reveals amplification of the ERBB2 (HER2) gene. Explain how this overexpression leads to oncogenesis via the cell cycle.
back:
HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase.
- Overexpression leads to constitutive growth signaling.
- Increases Cyclin D levels.
- Accelerates transition through the G1/S checkpoint.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the molecular consequences of a 'gain-of-function' mutation in Cyclin D1 with a 'loss-of-function' mutation in p16 (INK4a).
back:
- Cyclin D1 (Oncogene): Over-activates CDKs to drive the cycle forward.
- p16 (Tumor Suppressor): Normally inhibits CDK4/6; its loss removes a vital brake on Rb phosphorylation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between the G0 phase (quiescence) and permanent cell cycle arrest (senescence) in the context of oncogenesis.
back:
G0 (Quiescence): Reversible resting state; cells can re-enter cycle (e.g., hepatocytes).
- Senescence: Irreversible arrest often mediated by p53/p16; prevents damaged/aged cells from becoming neoplastic.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: State the consequence of a defective Mitotic (M-phase) spindle checkpoint on genomic stability in malignant cells.
back:
Failure results in chromosomal instability.
- Leads to aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number).
- Facilitates the rapid accumulation of multiple genetic hits required for tumor progression.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: In the context of tumor growth kinetics, the term used to describe the ratio of cells actively undergoing replication compared to those in the resting G0 phase is the [___].
back:
• Growth Fraction.
• High-growth-fraction tumors are generally more susceptible to cell cycle-specific (CCS) agents.
• As tumors enlarge, this fraction typically decreases (Gompertzian kinetics).

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 55-year-old male is diagnosed with a solid tumor. Genetic analysis reveals a mutation in a protein that normally halts the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint to allow for DNA repair. This tumor suppressor, mutated in nearly 50% of cancers, is [___].
back:
• p53 protein.
• It induces apoptosis or cell cycle arrest.
• Loss of function allows damaged DNA to replicate, facilitating oncogenic progression.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the biological reason why malignant cells in the G0 phase are typically resistant to antimetabolite chemotherapy drugs.
back:
• Antimetabolites (e.g., 5-FU, Methotrexate) are S-phase specific.
• G0 is a non-dividing resting state.
• Cells in G0 lack the active DNA synthesis processes that these drugs target.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the effectiveness of Cell Cycle-Specific (CCS) agents versus Cell Cycle-Nonspecific (CCNS) agents in treating a large, dormant tumor mass with low growth fraction.
back:
• CCS agents: Ineffective; they require active division (e.g., S or M phase).
• CCNS agents (e.g., Cyclophosphamide): Highly effective; they cross-link DNA regardless of the cell's cycling status.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the primary phase of the cell cycle where the genome is replicated and where antimetabolites exert their maximum cytotoxic effect.
back:
• S phase (Synthesis phase).
• It involves the doubling of DNA.
• Antimetabolites inhibit DNA polymerase or incorporate into DNA to terminate chain elongation.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Microtubule inhibitors, such as Vincristine and the Taxanes, lead to oncogenic cell death by specifically arresting the cycle during the [___] phase.
back:
• M phase (Mitosis).
• These drugs disrupt the mitotic spindle apparatus.
• Failure of chromosomal segregation triggers apoptosis.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A large abdominal mass is found to have non-exponential growth, with the growth fraction decreasing exponentially as the tumor size increases. This specific mathematical model of tumor regression and growth is known as [___].
back:
• Gompertzian Growth.
• Initial growth is rapid but slows as nutrients and oxygen become limited.
• Influences the need for debulking surgery prior to chemotherapy.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe the cellular events occurring during the G2 phase and identify the specific antitumor antibiotic that causes cells to accumulate in this phase.
back:
• G2 phase: Synthesis of cellular components and enzymes required for mitosis.
• Bleomycin: Specifically targets G2-M transition.
• Disruption at this point prevents the cell from entering division.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
coreConcept: G1 vs S phase metabolic role
front: Distinguish between the G1 and S phases regarding their roles in the metabolic preparation for cell division.
back:
• G1 phase: Synthesis of RNA, proteins, and enzymes needed for DNA replication.
• S phase: Actual replication of the DNA genome.
• Length of G1 varies most among different tumor types.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: List the role of biological 'checkpoints' within the cell cycle and their significance in preventing neoplastic transformation.
back:
• Checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M) monitor DNA integrity.
• They arrest the cycle for repair or trigger apoptosis.
• Abnormalities in these regulators allow unchecked proliferation of mutated cells.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The tumor suppressor protein often termed the 'guardian of the genome,' which triggers cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage, is [___].
back:
• p53 protein
• Acts at the G1/S checkpoint
• Induces p21 to inhibit Cyclin-CDK complexes
• Prevents replication of damaged genetic material

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A young child presents with leukocoria. Biopsy confirms a tumor resulting from a mutation in a gene that normally inhibits the E2F transcription factor. Identify the gene and its cell cycle role.
back:
• Rb (Retinoblastoma) gene
• Prevents G1 to S phase progression
• Sequesters E2F transcription factor when hypophosphorylated
• Loss of function leads to uncontrolled S-phase entry

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the mechanism by which Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) are regulated to ensure orderly progression through the cell cycle.
back:
• Activation requires binding with specific Cyclins
• Regulated by phosphorylation and dephosphorylation
• Inhibited by CDK inhibitors (e.g., p21, p16)
• Cyclin levels fluctuate via ubiquitin-proteasome degradation

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the roles of proto-oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes in the development of malignancy.
back:
• Proto-oncogenes: Require gain-of-function (one allele); drive cell growth (e.g., RAS)
• Tumor Suppressors: Require loss-of-function (two hits); lose inhibitory control (e.g., p53)
• Oncogenes are like gas pedals; tumor suppressors are brakes

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe the significance of the G1/S restriction point in preventing tumorigenesis.
back:
• Primary decision point for cellular division
• Monitors DNA integrity and nutrient availability
• Controlled by Rb and p53 proteins
• Failure allows cells with DNA damage to replicate

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The CDK inhibitor protein induced by p53 to cause cell cycle arrest following DNA damage is [___].
back:
• p21 (WAF1/CIP1)
• Potent inhibitor of CDK2 and CDK4
• Halts cycle in G1 to allow for repair
• Inactivation leads to genomic instability

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A patient with a strong family history of early-onset sarcomas and breast cancer is diagnosed with a germline mutation in p53. Name the syndrome and its cellular consequence.
back:
• Li-Fraumeni Syndrome
• Defective DNA damage sensing
• Accumulation of mutations across multiple cell lines
• High risk of multiple primary malignancies

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Detail the process by which a failure in the spindle assembly checkpoint (M-phase) contributes to oncogenesis.
back:
• Monitors proper attachment of chromosomes to spindles
• Failure leads to aneuploidy (abnormal chromosome number)
• Causes loss of tumor suppressors or gain of oncogenes
• Promotes genetic instability in daughter cells

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between cellular quiescence (G0) and senescence in the context of cell cycle arrest.
back:
• Quiescence: Reversible entry into G0; occurs during nutrient deprivation
• Senescence: Irreversible exit from cycle; occurs due to telomere shortening or damage
• Both serve as barriers to uncontrolled tumor growth

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the cell cycle phase where DNA synthesis occurs and why it is highly susceptible to oncogenic transformation.
back:
• S phase (Synthesis)
• DNA is unwound and vulnerable to damage
• Replication errors can become permanent mutations
• Faulty proofreading mechanisms lead to driver mutations

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: The protein often referred to as the 'guardian of the genome' that arrests the cell cycle in G1 upon detecting DNA damage is [___].
back:
• p53 protein.
• Induces p21 to inhibit Cyclin-CDK complexes.
• Triggers DNA repair or apoptosis (via Bax pathway) if damage is irreparable.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 4-year-old child presents with a white pupillary reflex (leukocoria). A mutation in a gene governing the G1/S transition is identified. This gene's protein normally sequesters which transcription factor?
back:
• E2F transcription factor.
• The gene is RB1 (Retinoblastoma gene).
• Hypophosphorylated Rb binds E2F, preventing the cell from entering the S-phase.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Explain the specific role of Cyclin-Dependent Kinases (CDKs) in facilitating oncogenic cell cycle progression when dysregulated.
back:
• CDKs phosphorylate target proteins to drive the cycle.
• Require binding to specific Cyclins for activation.
• Mutations cause constitutive activation, allowing cells to bypass critical growth-control checkpoints.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Contrast the cellular inheritance patterns and effects of 'Gain-of-Function' mutations in proto-oncogenes versus 'Loss-of-Function' in tumor suppressor genes.
back:
• Proto-oncogenes: Mutation in one allele (dominant) causes excessive growth signaling.
• Tumor Suppressors: Both alleles must be inactivated (Two-Hit Hypothesis) to remove cell cycle 'brakes'.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the inhibitory protein induced by p53 that directly halts the cell cycle by blocking CDK2 and CDK4, thereby preventing Rb phosphorylation.
back:
• p21 (Cip1/Waf1).
• Acts as a CDK inhibitor (CKI).
• Maintains the Rb protein in its active, hypophosphorylated state to prevent S-phase entry.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: During the cell cycle, the transition from the G2 phase to the M phase is primarily regulated by the [___] complex.
back:
• Cyclin B-CDK1 complex (Mitosis-Promoting Factor).
• Overexpression leads to premature mitosis and chromosomal instability.
• Crucial for checking completion of DNA replication.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: A 25-year-old patient with a history of various primary tumors (sarcoma, breast cancer, leukemia) is diagnosed with Li-Fraumeni syndrome. This condition represents a failure in which cellular process?
back:
• DNA damage checkpoint control and apoptosis.
• Caused by germline mutation in TP53.
• Resultant inability to eliminate cells with genomic instability leads to multiple malignancies.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Describe how the hyperphosphorylation of the Retinoblastoma (Rb) protein by Cyclin D/CDK4 promotes tumorigenesis.
back:
• Hyperphosphorylation releases the E2F transcription factor.
• Free E2F activates genes required for DNA synthesis.
• Excessive hyperphosphorylation leads to autonomous, unregulated cell division.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Distinguish between the biological consequences of MDM2 amplification and p16(INK4a) deletion in the context of the cell cycle.
back:
• MDM2 Amplification: Causes excessive p53 degradation, effectively silencing the G1 checkpoint.
• p16 Deletion: Removes CDK4/6 inhibition, resulting in constant Rb inactivation and replication.

category: Describe how abnormalities in the cell cycle lead to oncogenesis
front: Identify the specific late G1-phase point beyond which a cell becomes committed to DNA replication regardless of extracellular growth factor availability.
back:
• Restriction Point (R-point).
• Controlled by the Rb/E2F molecular switch.
• Dysregulation of the R-point is a nearly universal feature of human cancer cells.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The metabolic byproduct of nucleic acid catabolism that precipitates in renal tubules during tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) is [___].
back:
• Uric acid (Hyperuricemia)
• Derived from purine breakdown
• Causes obstructive uropathy
• Managed with aggressive hydration and allopurinol

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient with bulky non-Hodgkin lymphoma develops cardiac arrhythmias 18 hours after starting Rituximab. Labs show hyperkalemia and hypocalcemia. Identify the likely pathophysiology.
back:
• Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS)
• Rapid release of intracellular contents
• Common in high-turnover malignancies
• Triggers acute metabolic emergencies

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism behind the development of secondary hypocalcemia during an acute episode of tumour lysis syndrome.
back:
• Hyperphosphatemia from cell lysis
• Phosphate binds ionized calcium
• Forms calcium-phosphate crystals
• Crystals deposit in kidneys and soft tissues

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Distinguish between the pharmacological mechanisms of Allopurinol and Rasburicase in the management of TLS-induced hyperuricemia.
back:
• Allopurinol: Inhibits xanthine oxidase; prevents new uric acid synthesis
• Rasburicase: Recombinant urate oxidase; degrades existing uric acid into allantoin
• Rasburicase is faster for established hyperuricemia

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the primary intracellular anion released during malignant cell destruction that leads to 'hyperphosphatasemia' and subsequent renal damage in TLS.
back:
• Phosphate (Hyperphosphatemia)
• Exceeds renal excretory capacity
• Promotes calcium-phosphate precipitation
• Major cause of acute kidney injury in TLS

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The electrolyte abnormality in tumour lysis syndrome most immediately life-threatening to cardiac conduction and rhythm is [___].
back:
• Hyperkalemia
• Caused by massive intracellular potassium release
• Risk of peaked T waves and cardiac arrest
• Requires urgent stabilization with calcium gluconate

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A 15-year-old with Burkitt lymphoma is started on aggressive intravenous hydration and xanthine oxidase inhibitors prior to chemotherapy. State the primary goal of this prophylaxis.
back:
• Prevention of Tumour Lysis Syndrome
• Promotes uric acid solubility and excretion
• Dilutes intracellular toxins
• Prevents obstructive crystalline nephropathy

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe the catabolic pathway by which malignant cell destruction leads to elevated systemic uric acid levels.
back:
• Release of DNA/RNA nucleic acids
• Purine (adenine/guanine) degradation to xanthine
• Xanthine oxidase converts xanthine to uric acid
• High turnover in TLS overwhelms clearance

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the typical clinical risk of TLS in high-grade hematologic malignancies versus slow-growing solid adenocarcinomas.
back:
• High-grade (Burkitt/ALL): High risk due to rapid turnover
• Solid tumors: Rare; occurs only in highly sensitive/bulky disease
• Reflects differences in tumor burden and growth fraction

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: List the four hallmark metabolic derangements that constitute the laboratory diagnosis of Tumour Lysis Syndrome.
back:
• Hyperuricemia
• Hyperkalemia
• Hyperphosphatemia
• Hypocalcemia

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In the management of tumour lysis syndrome, the recombinant enzyme [___] converts insoluble uric acid into highly soluble allantoin.
back:
* Rasburicase
* Recombinant urate oxidase
* Prevents uric acid nephropathy
* Indicated for high risk of lysis

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A 12-year-old with Burkitt's lymphoma develops oliguria and muscle cramps after chemotherapy. Labs show elevated K+, PO4, and urate. This metabolic emergency is [___].
back:
* Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS)
* Result of massive cytolysis
* Triggers severe electrolyte disturbances
* Potential for acute kidney injury

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the biochemical basis for secondary hypocalcemia during the acute phase of tumour lysis syndrome.
back:
* Rapid release of intracellular phosphorus
* High serum phosphate binds ionized calcium
* Leads to calcium-phosphate precipitation
* Symptoms include tetany and arrhythmias

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the pharmacodynamic roles of Allopurinol and Rasburicase in managing malignancy-related hyperuricemia.
back:
* Allopurinol: Inhibits xanthine oxidase/production
* Rasburicase: Enzymatically breaks down existing urate
* Allopurinol is prophylactic; Rasburicase treats active lysis
* Rasburicase creates more soluble allantoin

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the primary pathophysiological event causing obstructive renal failure in tumour lysis syndrome.
back:
* Intratubular crystallization of uric acid
* Deposition of calcium-phosphate complexes
* Mechanical obstruction of distal tubules
* Elevated intraluminal pressure/decreased GFR

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The electrolyte disturbance released during tumor cell lysis that represents the most immediate threat to cardiac rhythm is [___].
back:
* Hyperkalemia
* Risk of ventricular arrhythmias/arrest
* Requires serial EKG monitoring
* Managed with insulin and dextrose

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A lymphoma patient receives aggressive pre-treatment hydration. Describe how this prevents uric acid-induced acute kidney injury.
back:
* Increases tubular flow rate
* Dilutes urinary solute concentration
* Reduces transit time for crystal formation
* Enhances renal urate clearance

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Detail the metabolic transformation occurring when Rasburicase acts upon its biological substrate.
back:
* Uric acid + O2 + H2O → Allantoin
* Allantoin is highly water-soluble
* Eliminated easily by the kidneys
* Unlike urate, allantoin does not precipitate

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Distinguish between the urinary pH conditions that promote uric acid precipitation versus those promoting calcium phosphate precipitation.
back:
* Uric acid: Low pH (acidic) favors precipitation
* Calcium phosphate: High pH (alkaline) favors precipitation
* Aggressive alkalinization may worsen phosphate precipitation
* Hydration remains the primary management

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: State the two haematological malignancies most frequently associated with the development of spontaneous or treatment-induced tumour lysis syndrome.
back:
* Burkitt's Lymphoma
* Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL)
* High tumor burden/rapid turnover
* Requires close laboratory monitoring

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In tumour lysis syndrome, the rapid breakdown of nucleic acids leads to the excessive production of [___], which may cause acute obstructive uropathy.
back: Uric acid. Excess urate precipitates in renal tubules under acidic conditions. This leads to acute kidney injury (AKI). Prophylaxis includes aggressive hydration and xanthine oxidase inhibitors.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient with bulky Burkitt lymphoma develops muscle cramps, tetany, and a positive Chvostek sign 24 hours after starting chemotherapy. Identify the underlying metabolic derangement.
back: Hypocalcemia. This occurs because the massive release of intracellular phosphate binds to ionized calcium. The resulting calcium-phosphate crystals deposit in soft tissues and kidneys, further contributing to renal failure.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe the pharmacological mechanism by which Rasburicase effectively manages hyperuricemia during the treatment of hematologic malignancies.
back: Rasburicase is a recombinant urate oxidase enzyme. It catalyzes the conversion of poorly soluble uric acid into allantoin. Allantoin is highly water-soluble and easily excreted by the kidneys.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the clinical utility of Allopurinol versus Rasburicase in the management of high-risk tumour lysis syndrome.
back: Allopurinol prevents new uric acid synthesis by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. Rasburicase actively degrades existing uric acid. Rasburicase is preferred for patients with existing high urate levels or high tumor burden.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain why aggressive intravenous hydration is the primary preventative measure for patients at risk of metabolic collapse following chemotherapy.
back: Hydration maintains high urine flow, increasing glomerular filtration. It dilutes the concentration of uric acid and phosphate in renal tubules, preventing crystal precipitation and subsequent acute kidney injury.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: According to Cairo-Bishop criteria, Laboratory TLS is defined by at least two metabolic abnormalities occurring within [___] hours of initiating therapy.
back: Three to seven days. The criteria include a 25% change from baseline in serum levels of potassium, phosphorus, uric acid, or calcium. This classification helps identify early-stage metabolic risk.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: During induction therapy for AML, a patient's labs show hyperkalemia and peaked T-waves on ECG. Specify the most immediate life-threatening risk to the patient.
back: Cardiac arrhythmias. Rapid release of intracellular potassium exceeds renal clearance capacity. This can lead to sudden cardiac arrest if not managed with insulin/glucose or calcium gluconate.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Detail the metabolic sequence of events that leads to acute kidney injury specifically caused by hyperphosphatemia during tumor cell necrosis.
back: Dying tumor cells release organic phosphorus. This causes hyperphosphatemia, leading to calcium-phosphate crystal formation. These crystals precipitate in the renal medulla, causing obstruction and acute nephrocalcinosis.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Distinguish between the target of Allopurinol and Febuxostat in the prevention of hyperuricemia.
back: Both inhibit xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol is a purine analog, while Febuxostat is a non-purine selective inhibitor. Febuxostat is an alternative for patients who cannot tolerate allopurinol's side effects.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the byproduct of uric acid degradation that is 5-10 times more soluble than urate, facilitating renal clearance.
back: Allantoin. It is the end-product of the reaction catalyzed by urate oxidase. Its high solubility prevents the formation of crystals in the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The electrolyte abnormality in Tumor Lysis Syndrome that results from the release of intracellular nucleic acid breakdown products is [___].
back:
Hyperuricemia.
* Caused by catabolism of nuclear purines.
* Leads to uric acid crystal deposition in renal tubules.
* Risks obstructive acute kidney injury.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient with Burkitt lymphoma develops oliguria and peaked T-waves on ECG 24 hours after starting chemotherapy. Identify the most likely metabolic emergency.
back:
Tumor Lysis Syndrome (TLS).
* Rapid malignant cell destruction releases intracellular contents.
* Hyperkalemia causes the peaked T-waves.
* Renal failure results from crystalline nephropathy.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the biochemical basis for secondary hypocalcemia observed during rapid tumor cell necrosis.
back:
Phosphate-Calcium Binding.
* Intracellular phosphate release causes severe hyperphosphatemia.
* Excess phosphate binds serum calcium ions.
* Results in calcium-phosphate precipitation in kidneys and tissues.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the enzymatic mechanisms of Allopurinol versus Rasburicase in managing hyperuricemia during oncology treatment.
back:
Allopurinol vs. Rasburicase.
* Allopurinol: Inhibits xanthine oxidase to prevent uric acid formation.
* Rasburicase: Recombinant urate oxidase that converts existing uric acid to soluble allantoin.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Specify the most effective physiological strategy to prevent uric acid crystal-induced nephropathy in high-risk lymphoma patients.
back:
Aggressive Intravenous Hydration.
* Increases urine flow and glomerular filtration.
* Dilutes uric acid and phosphate concentrations.
* Prevents solute precipitation in the renal tubules.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In Tumor Lysis Syndrome, the precipitation of [___] crystals in the renal tubules is the primary cause of acute renal failure when phosphate levels are high.
back:
Calcium phosphate.
* Formed when the calcium-phosphate product exceeds solubility.
* Leads to nephrocalcinosis and obstructive uropathy.
* Exacerbated by low serum calcium.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: An ALL patient on chemotherapy presents with tetany and a positive Chvostek sign. Identify the metabolic driver of these neuromuscular symptoms.
back:
Hypocalcemia.
* Secondary to hyperphosphatemia-induced calcium precipitation.
* Low ionized calcium increases neuromuscular irritability.
* Presents as tetany, seizures, or arrhythmias.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe how Rasburicase alters the excretion pathway of nitrogenous waste compared to the physiological human pathway.
back:
Urate to Allantoin Conversion.
* Humans lack the urate oxidase enzyme.
* Rasburicase catalyzes uric acid into allantoin.
* Allantoin is 10 times more soluble and easily excreted.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Differentiate between the intracellular origins of hyperkalemia and hyperuricemia in Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
back:
Cation vs. Nucleic Acid Release.
* Hyperkalemia: Direct release of the primary intracellular cation.
* Hyperuricemia: Breakdown of nuclear DNA and RNA purines (adenine/guanine).

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the four hallmark metabolic derangements that define Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
back:
Laboratory Criteria.
* Hyperkalemia (Potassium).
* Hyperuricemia (Uric Acid).
* Hyperphosphatemia (Phosphate).
* Hypocalcemia (Calcium).

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In tumour lysis syndrome, the precipitation of [___] crystals in the renal tubules is a primary cause of acute kidney injury.
back:
* Uric acid.
* This results from the rapid breakdown of nucleic acids into purines, which are then metabolized to urate, causing crystalline nephropathy.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient with Burkitt lymphoma develops muscle cramps and tetany 24 hours after starting chemotherapy. Which electrolyte disturbance in TLS is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
back:
* Hypocalcemia.
* This occurs as a secondary effect of hyperphosphatemia, where excess phosphate binds to systemic calcium, causing it to precipitate in tissues.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the biochemical rationale for the development of hyperuricemia during rapid tumour cell destruction.
back:
* Lysis releases large amounts of DNA/RNA.
* Nucleic acids are catabolized into purines (adenine/guanine).
* Xanthine oxidase converts these purines into uric acid, exceeding renal clearance.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the pharmacological mechanisms of Allopurinol and Rasburicase in the management of uric acid during TLS.
back:
* Allopurinol: Inhibits xanthine oxidase to prevent the formation of *new* uric acid.
* Rasburicase: A recombinant urate oxidase that converts *existing* uric acid into highly soluble allantoin.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe the clinical significance of aggressive intravenous hydration as a preventative measure for TLS-associated nephropathy.
back:
* Increases urine flow and glomerular filtration.
* Dilutes the concentration of uric acid and phosphate in renal tubules.
* Reduces the likelihood of crystal precipitation and obstructive uropathy.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias seen in TLS are primarily a consequence of [___].
back:
* Hyperkalemia.
* Intracellular potassium is released rapidly into the systemic circulation upon the lysis of a high volume of neoplastic cells.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Following chemotherapy for AML, a patient's labs show elevated LDH, uric acid, and phosphate. Identify the appropriate pharmacotherapy to rapidly reduce the established urate burden.
back:
* Rasburicase.
* Unlike allopurinol, rasburicase acts directly on existing uric acid to facilitate its conversion into allantoin for renal excretion.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe why hyperphosphatemia in TLS often leads to acute renal failure even if uric acid levels are controlled.
back:
* Released intracellular phosphate binds with calcium.
* Forms calcium-phosphate complexes that precipitate in the renal parenchyma.
* Results in nephrocalcinosis and acute tubular injury.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
coreConcept: Spurious Lab Findings in Hematologic Malignancy
front: Distinguish between the metabolic profiles of clinical Tumour Lysis Syndrome and Pseudo-Tumour Lysis Syndrome (spurious laboratory results).
back:
* TLS: Involves systemic metabolic derangements and acute renal impairment.
* Pseudo-TLS: Spurious elevations in potassium/phosphate occur in the test tube due to fragile cells lysing during blood draw (in vitro).

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the metabolic triad that defines the laboratory diagnosis of Tumour Lysis Syndrome.
back:
* Hyperuricemia.
* Hyperkalemia.
* Hyperphosphatemia.
* (Accompanied by secondary hypocalcemia).

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In tumour lysis syndrome, the rapid destruction of malignant cells leads to a systemic elevation of [___], which can precipitate in renal tubules alongside uric acid to cause acute kidney injury.
back:
Phosphate (Hyperphosphatemia)
- Released from intracellular nucleic acid breakdown.
- Forms calcium-phosphate crystals in the renal parenchyma.
- Managed with aggressive hydration and phosphate binders.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient undergoing induction chemotherapy for Burkitt lymphoma develops sudden onset oliguria and peaked T-waves on ECG. Laboratory results show markedly elevated LDH and uric acid. Describe the pathophysiological process leading to the cardiac findings in this patient.
back:
Hyperkalemic Cardiotoxicity
- Massive lysis releases intracellular potassium into the circulation.
- High serum potassium alters the resting membrane potential of myocytes.
- Leads to cardiac irritability, peaked T-waves, and potential asystole.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the clinical advantage of utilizing Rasburicase over Allopurinol for the management of hyperuricemia during an acute oncologic emergency.
back:
Urate Metabolism vs. Synthesis Inhibition
- Rasburicase: A recombinant urate oxidase that actively breaks down existing uric acid into highly soluble allantoin.
- Allopurinol: Inhibits xanthine oxidase, merely preventing the formation of new uric acid.
- Rasburicase provides rapid reduction of pre-existing urate levels.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Chemotherapy-Related Renal Failure
front: Contrast the electrolyte profile of acute Tumour Lysis Syndrome with that of Cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity, specifically regarding serum potassium and magnesium levels.
back:
Electrolyte Differentiation
- TLS: Presents with hyperkalemia and hyperphosphatemia due to massive intracellular release from ruptured cells.
- Cisplatin Toxicity: Typically causes hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia due to direct renal tubular damage and electrolyte wasting.
- TLS is a distributive excess; Cisplatin is a renal loss.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: State the clinical rationale for withholding intravenous calcium supplementation in a patient with asymptomatic hypocalcemia during the initial phase of tumour lysis syndrome.
back:
Prevention of Metastatic Calcification
- High serum phosphate levels increase the calcium-phosphate product.
- Administering calcium can trigger the precipitation of crystals in kidneys and soft tissues.
- Calcium is reserved for symptomatic tetany or life-threatening hyperkalemia with ECG changes.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: In cancer chemotherapy, the corticosteroid [___] is often utilized for its palliative effect of increasing appetite and promoting weight gain in cachectic patients.
back:
Prednisone
* Commonly used in palliative care regimens.
* Stimulates appetite and improves dietary intake.
* Helps reduce peritumoral edema and inflammation.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A 55-year-old male with metastatic lung cancer presents with worsening headaches and neurological deficits. Imaging shows multiple brain metastases with significant peritumoral edema. Which drug is used for symptom relief?
back:
Dexamethasone
* Reduces peritumoral cerebral edema effectively.
* Relieves intracranial pressure symptoms.
* Preferred due to minimal mineralocorticoid activity and high potency.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Explain how Megestrol acetate carries out its biological function as a palliative treatment in advanced malignancies.
back:
Megestrol Acetate Mechanism
* Progestational agent that stimulates appetite.
* Specifically used for palliation of cancer-related cachexia.
* Used in advanced breast and endometrial cancer management.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Contrast the primary goals of palliative chemotherapy with those of curative chemotherapy in advanced metastatic tumors.
back:
Treatment Goals Contrast
* Palliative: Relieve symptoms, improve quality of life, and prolong survival without eradication.
* Curative: Complete eradication of every neoplastic cell.
* Palliative care emphasizes minimal toxicity.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Name the class of drugs added to palliative regimens to prevent skeletal complications like fractures in patients with bone metastases.
back:
Bisphosphonates
* Examples: Zoledronic acid or Pamidronate.
* Inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
* Reduce bone pain and risk of pathological fractures.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: The GnRH analog used for the palliative management of advanced prostate cancer by inducing chemical castration is [___].
back:
Leuprolide
* Synthetic GnRH analog.
* Suppresses LH and FSH release via pituitary desensitization.
* Reduces testosterone to castration levels, relieving bone pain.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A patient with advanced prostate cancer experiences a transient increase in bone pain immediately after starting Leuprolide. Explain the phenomenon and the drug added to prevent it.
back:
Tumor Flare
* Initial GnRH stimulation causes a testosterone surge.
* Antiandrogens (e.g., Flutamide) are added to block receptors.
* Prevents acute worsening of metastatic symptoms.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: How do Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors (TKI) like Imatinib serve as palliative therapy in advanced Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumors (GIST)?
back:
Imatinib Palliation
* Inhibits the unregulated c-kit tyrosine kinase.
* Prevents downstream signaling for tumor cell proliferation.
* Regresses tumor size to alleviate gastrointestinal symptoms.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Distinguish between the palliative mechanisms of Bicalutamide and Leuprolide in metastatic prostate cancer.
back:
Hormonal Contrast
* Bicalutamide: Competitive antagonist at the androgen receptor.
* Leuprolide: Suppresses androgen production via the pituitary-gonadal axis.
* Both reduce androgenic growth stimulation.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Specify the role of glucocorticoids in the palliative management of bone pain associated with metastatic disease.
back:
Glucocorticoids for Pain
* Reduce inflammation around tumor sites.
* Decrease pressure on nerves and the spinal cord.
* Improve mood and sense of well-being.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The recombinant urate oxidase enzyme used to rapidly lower plasma uric acid by converting it into the highly soluble [___] is Rasburicase.
back:
* Allantoin.
* Conversion increases renal clearance of purine metabolites.
* Effectively bypasses the human metabolic deficiency of urate oxidase.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient with high-grade lymphoma develops muscle cramps, oliguria, and peaked T-waves on ECG 12 hours after chemotherapy. Identify the electrolyte imbalance causing these cardiac changes.
back:
* Hyperkalemia.
* Caused by massive release of intracellular potassium.
* Carries a high risk for life-threatening arrhythmias or sudden cardiac arrest.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of secondary hypocalcemia observed in Tumor Lysis Syndrome.
back:
* Rapid intracellular phosphate release leads to hyperphosphatemia.
* Excess phosphate complex with serum calcium, causing precipitation.
* Results in soft-tissue calcification and systemic depletion of ionized calcium.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the clinical utility and timing for Allopurinol versus Rasburicase in managing hyperuricemia during tumor debulking.
back:
* Allopurinol: Xanthine oxidase inhibitor used for prophylaxis to prevent new uric acid formation.
* Rasburicase: Urate oxidase enzyme used as rescue therapy to degrade existing uric acid.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Describe the mechanical pathophysiology by which hyperuricemia induces acute kidney injury in TLS.
back:
* Excess uric acid exceeds solubility in acidic renal tubular fluid.
* Crystals precipitate within distal tubules and collecting ducts.
* Leads to mechanical luminal obstruction and acute obstructive uropathy.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In patients with a known hypersensitivity to allopurinol, the non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor [___] is utilized for TLS prophylaxis.
back:
* Febuxostat.
* Potently inhibits uric acid production without purine-analog side effects.
* Used as an alternative prophylactic agent in high-risk patients.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A pediatric patient with leukemia develops tetany following their first dose of Rituximab. Explain the relationship between intracellular phosphate release and this neuromuscular finding.
back:
* Massive phosphate release creates hyperphosphatemia.
* High phosphate binds serum calcium, causing rapid precipitation.
* The resulting acute hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular irritability and tetany.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Detail the physiological rationale for aggressive intravenous hydration as a first-line intervention in TLS management.
back:
* Increases glomerular filtration rate and tubular flow.
* Dilutes the concentrations of phosphorus and uric acid.
* Minimizes intratubular crystal precipitation and prevents mechanical renal damage.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Distinguish between the metabolic targets of Allopurinol and Febuxostat in the prevention of hyperuricemia.
back:
* Allopurinol: A purine-analog inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.
* Febuxostat: A non-purine-analog inhibitor of xanthine oxidase.
* Both prevent synthesis but differ in chemical structure and hypersensitivity risks.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the four hallmark metabolic disturbances that define Laboratory Tumor Lysis Syndrome (Cairo-Bishop Criteria).
back:
* Hyperuricemia.
* Hyperkalemia.
* Hyperphosphatemia.
* Hypocalcemia.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: To mitigate the cumulative nephrotoxicity associated with high-dose Cisplatin therapy, the cytoprotective agent [___] is utilized as a reactive species scavenger.
back:
* Amifostine.
* Acts as a prodrug neutralized by alkaline phosphatase.
* Scavenges free radicals in normal tissues.
* Reduces renal and ototoxicity.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: A 55-year-old patient being treated for colorectal cancer with Irinotecan develops acute diaphoresis, salivation, and abdominal cramping within 30 minutes of infusion. State the immediate pharmacological management.
back:
* Atropine.
* Mechanism: Manages the early cholinergic syndrome (diarrhea/cramping) caused by Irinotecan inhibiting acetylcholinesterase.
* Dose: Intravenous or subcutaneous injection.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: Explain the mechanism by which Ondansetron prevents the severe nausea and vomiting (CINV) associated with highly emetogenic chemotherapy like Cisplatin.
back:
* 5-HT3 receptor antagonism.
* Blocks serotonin receptors on vagal afferents in the GI tract.
* Blocks receptors in the Chemoreceptor Trigger Zone (CTZ) and Solitary Tract Nucleus.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: Contrast the management of 'Early-onset' versus 'Late-onset' diarrhea associated with Irinotecan therapy.
back:
* Early-onset: Cholinergic mechanism; treated with Atropine.
* Late-onset: Secretary/toxic mechanism; treated with high-dose Loperamide.
* Note: Late diarrhea can be life-threatening and occurs days after treatment.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: In advanced cancer patients suffering from severe cachexia and anorexia, which progestational agent is specifically indicated to improve appetite and promote weight gain?
back:
* Megestrol Acetate.
* Stimulates appetite through unknown hypothalamic mechanisms.
* Leads to increased fat and muscle mass accumulation.
* Often used in palliative oncology.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: For the prevention of acute renal failure in Tumor Lysis Syndrome, the recombinant enzyme [___] is preferred for its ability to convert insoluble uric acid into highly soluble allantoin.
back:
* Rasburicase.
* Recombinant urate oxidase.
* Unlike allopurinol, it eliminates existing uric acid.
* Prevents urate crystal deposition in renal tubules.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: A 40-year-old with a primary glioblastoma presents with sudden worsening of headache, papilledema, and projectile vomiting. Beyond surgery, which pharmacological intervention is prioritized to reduce peritumoral edema?
back:
* High-dose Dexamethasone.
* Mechanism: Reduces capillary permeability in the blood-brain barrier.
* Effect: Rapidly decreases intracranial pressure and improves neurological symptoms.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: Describe how Zoledronic acid (a Bisphosphonate) provides clinical benefit to a patient with metastatic bone disease from breast cancer.
back:
* Inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.
* Reduces risk of 'Skeletal Related Events' (fractures/pain).
* Promotes osteoclast apoptosis.
* Prevents tumor-induced hypercalcemia.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: Distinguish between the clinical roles of Filgrastim (G-CSF) and Sargramostim (GM-CSF) in a patient following autologous bone marrow transplantation.
back:
* Filgrastim: Specifically stimulates neutrophil recovery.
* Sargramostim: Stimulates recovery of multiple lines (neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages).
* Both reduce duration of severe neutropenia and infection risk.

category: Describe the drugs used beside surgical resection of various tumours to treat complications
front: Identify the two specific nutritional supplements mandatory for administration with Pralatrexate or Pemetrexed to minimize dose-limiting hematologic and GI toxicities.
back:
* Folic Acid (oral).
* Vitamin B12 (intramuscular injection).
* Rationale: Reduces the frequency of severe myelosuppression and mucositis while preserving therapeutic efficacy.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: The hallmark biochemical derangement in tumour lysis syndrome characterized by the systemic accumulation of purine catabolites is [___].
back: - Hyperuricemia. - Caused by rapid nucleic acid degradation. - Leads to obstructive uropathy via crystal formation. - Managed with aggressive hydration and urate oxidase.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: A patient being treated for high-grade non-Hodgkin lymphoma develops sudden onset oliguria and laboratory values showing elevated serum uric acid and phosphate. Name the most likely acute complication.
back: - Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS). - Occurs after chemotherapy for bulky or high-turnover tumors. - Hallmarks include hyperkalemia, hyperuricemia, and hyperphosphatemia. - Leads to acute kidney injury.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Detail the metabolic process by which rapid cytolysis leads to the symptomatic neuromuscular excitability known as tetany.
back: - Secondary Hypocalcemia. - Intracellular phosphate is released in large quantities. - Phosphate binds serum ionized calcium. - Resulting calcium-phosphate crystals deposit in tissues, lowering circulating calcium.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Distinguish the pharmacological mechanism of action of Rasburicase from that of Allopurinol in the management of malignancy-induced hyperuricemia.
back: - Allopurinol: Prevents uric acid synthesis by inhibiting xanthine oxidase. - Rasburicase: Directly degrades existing uric acid into allantoin. - Allopurinol is prophylactic; Rasburicase is for active lysis.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Identify the primary site of tubular damage caused by the precipitation of uric acid crystals during massive tumour cell breakdown.
back: - Distal Renal Tubules. - Uric acid is least soluble in acidic environments. - Precipitation occurs primarily in the distal tubules and collecting ducts. - Leads to intratubular obstruction.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: In the management of tumour lysis syndrome, the conversion of uric acid into the highly soluble metabolite [___] is facilitated by the enzyme Rasburicase.
back: - Allantoin. - Recombinant urate oxidase (Rasburicase) catalyzes this conversion. - Allantoin is significantly more soluble than uric acid. - Facilitates safe renal excretion of purine metabolites.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: During induction chemotherapy for leukemia, a patient presents with peaked T-waves on ECG and a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L. Determine the cellular origin of this electrolyte shift.
back: - Intracellular Efflux. - Malignant cells contain high concentrations of potassium. - Rapid cell membrane rupture releases potassium into the extracellular space. - Exceeds renal excretory capacity, causing arrhythmias.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Explain the pathophysiological relationship between hyperphosphatasemia and the development of acute renal failure in systemic lysis.
back: - Calcium-Phosphate Precipitation. - Sudden phosphate release binds systemic calcium. - Insoluble crystals precipitate within the renal parenchyma. - Causes nephrocalcinosis and acute tubular necrosis, contributing to renal failure.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Contrast the impact of Hyperkalemia versus Hypocalcemia on the cardiac conduction system as seen in tumour lysis syndrome.
back: - Hyperkalemia: Causes peaked T-waves, PR prolongation, and QRS widening. - Hypocalcemia: Prolongs the QT interval. - Both significantly increase the risk of lethal ventricular arrhythmias.

category: in tumour lysis syndrome
front: Enumerate the four specific laboratory criteria used to confirm a diagnosis of Tumour Lysis Syndrome according to the Cairo-Bishop system.
back: - Hyperuricemia: Uric acid >8 mg/dL. - Hyperkalemia: Potassium >6 mEq/L. - Hyperphosphatemia: Phosphate >4.5 mg/dL. - Hypocalcemia: Serum calcium <7 mg/dL.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: In palliative oncological care, the corticosteroid [___] is frequently utilized to stimulate appetite and promote weight gain in patients with cachexia due to advanced malignancies.
back:
* Prednisone
* Induces an orexigenic (appetite-stimulating) effect
* Enhances energy levels and general well-being
* Commonly used for symptomatic relief in terminal cases

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A 55-year-old male with metastatic lung cancer presents with severe headaches and projectile vomiting. Imaging reveals brain metastases with significant peritumoral edema. Identify the primary palliative steroid used to manage this swelling.
back:
* Dexamethasone
* Reduces vasogenic cerebral edema
* Decreases intracranial pressure (ICP)
* Has minimal mineralocorticoid activity, making it ideal for high-dose neuro-palliation

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Explain the pharmacological reason for preferring the prodrug Prednisone over active Prednisolone in a pregnant patient requiring palliative steroid therapy.
back:
* The fetal liver cannot convert Prednisone (prodrug) to active Prednisolone
* Maternal placental enzymes (11-beta-HSD) inactivate any maternal prednisolone
* Minimizes systemic steroid exposure to the developing fetus

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A terminal patient suffers from severe bone pain due to osteolytic breast cancer metastases. Distinguish the role of Bisphosphonates from Corticosteroids in this palliative setting.
back:
* Bisphosphonates: Inhibit osteoclasts to reduce bone resorption and prevent pathological fractures.
* Corticosteroids: Rapidly reduce inflammation and edema around tumor sites, alleviating pressure-related pain.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Define the primary therapeutic objective of "Palliation" when initiating systemic chemotherapy in a patient with Stage IV disseminated malignancy.
back:
* Symptom alleviation (e.g., pain, obstruction)
* Maintenance of the best possible Quality of Life (QOL)
* Extension of survival without the expectation of a total cure
* Managing cancer as a chronic, controllable disease

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: To prevent respiratory distress syndrome in a preterm infant during maternal oncological care, the glucocorticoid [___] is administered to the mother to accelerate fetal lung maturation.
back:
* Betamethasone (or Dexamethasone)
* Stimulates fetal surfactant production
* Requires high glucocorticoid activity for efficacy
* Administered intramuscularly within 48 hours of expected delivery

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A patient with advanced mediastinal lymphoma experiences superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome and severe dyspnea. Explain how palliative chemotherapy relieves these symptoms.
back:
* Cytoreduction (Debulking): Rapidly shrinks the tumor mass
* Relieves extrinsic compression of the SVC and major airways
* Restores venous return and improves ventilation/perfusion

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Contrast the palliative utility of Dexamethasone with traditional opioids in the management of neuropathic pain from tumor invasion.
back:
* Dexamethasone: Reduces inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF) and stabilizes membranes to decrease nerve irritation.
* Opioids: Act on central/peripheral receptors to modify pain perception without addressing the local inflammatory cause.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Distinguish between the palliative use of Capecitabine and intravenous 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) in an elderly patient with metastatic colorectal cancer.
back:
* Capecitabine: Oral prodrug, tumor-specific activation via thymidine phosphorylase, allows home-based palliative care.
* 5-FU: Requires intravenous access/infusion pumps, associated with higher incidences of systemic mucositis.

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Identify the primary mechanism by which Metoclopramide assists in the palliative care of a cancer patient with malignant gastric stasis.
back:
* Dopamine (D2) receptor antagonist
* Prokinetic effect: Increases gastric emptying and upper GI motility
* Relieves nausea caused by delayed stomach emptying (gastroparesis)

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: In palliative oncological care, the glucocorticoid [___] is frequently utilized specifically for its ability to stimulate appetite and promote weight gain in cachectic patients.
back:
• Prednisone
• Increases caloric intake
• Improves overall sense of well-being
• Reduces inflammation-related anorexia

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A 72-year-old male with metastatic prostate cancer presents with debilitating bone pain. Which drug class provides palliation by desensitizing pituitary receptors to inhibit LH release?
back:
• GnRH (LHRH) Agonists
• Example: Leuprolide or Goserelin
• Reduces testosterone to castration levels
• Effectively relieves metastatic bone pain

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which high-dose Dexamethasone provides palliative relief in patients with primary or metastatic brain tumors.
back:
• Reduces peritumoral cerebral edema
• Decreases capillary permeability in the CNS
• Lowers intracranial pressure
• Alleviates associated headaches and neurologic deficits

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Contrast the palliative utility of Mitoxantrone with standard LHRH agonists in the management of advanced prostate carcinoma.
back:
• Mitoxantrone: Used for hormone-refractory cases to relieve bone pain
• LHRH Agonists: First-line hormonal palliation via testosterone suppression
• Mitoxantrone targets topoisomerase II specifically for symptomatic relief

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Identify the primary indication for utilizing progestins, such as Megestrol acetate, in the setting of palliative oncology.
back:
• Metastatic hormone-responsive breast cancer
• Metastatic endometrial carcinoma
• Second-line palliation after aromatase inhibitors
• Also used to treat cancer-related cachexia

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: During palliative therapy for various tumors, [___] are often co-administered with long-term corticosteroids to inhibit bone resorption and prevent fractures.
back:
• Bisphosphonates
• Counteract suppressed intestinal calcium absorption
• Manage glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis
• Reduce risk of skeletal-related events

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: A postmenopausal woman with metastatic breast cancer requires palliation. If she has a high risk of thromboembolism, which class of agents is preferred over Tamoxifen?
back:
• Aromatase Inhibitors
• Examples: Anastrozole, Letrozole
• Devoid of estrogenic side effects
• Lower risk of endometrial cancer and clots

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Describe the physiological process by which Prednisone acts as a palliative agent specifically in hematologic malignancies like lymphomas.
back:
• Induces lymphocytolysis of neoplastic B and T cells
• Triggers apoptosis in lymphoid tissue
• Redistributes lymphocytes from circulation to lymphoid depots
• Reduces tumor-associated inflammatory symptoms

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Distinguish between the palliative roles of Flutamide and Leuprolide in managing advanced prostatic symptoms.
back:
• Flutamide: Competes for the androgen receptor (Antagonist)
• Leuprolide: Inhibits LH release via pituitary desensitization (Agonist)
• Both achieve androgen deprivation to relieve bone pain

category: Describe the drugs used for palliative therapy in various tumours
front: Beyond appetite stimulation, what is the major palliative role of Dexamethasone regarding the systemic side effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy?
